head: 5ba16c3
note: Eleven READ-ONLY finders over the 86 non-docs files that changed between b802686 and 5ba16c3 — the round-6 tree, which is almost entirely fixes to round 5s fixes, plus one brand-new design (the two-number AI cost split) and one large deletion (the child-refresh recovery removal). Disjoint file lists whose union was verified to equal the diff exactly before dispatch (L-048, L-052). Finders returned fix_touches (every file a fix would change, including files outside the diff) and, new this round, claim_under_review: the comment, test name or premise in the round-6 change that the finding shows to be false. 60 findings: 2 high, 29 medium, 29 low, plus 78 properties the finders attacked and could not break. Recorded BEFORE any fixing.

findings.title: The child space's screen-privacy debt can be recorded AFTER the 'active' event that is supposed to settle it, so a paired tablet keeps refusing screenshots, recording and casting
findings.claim_under_review: "A paired tablet locked on its way out is owed the child space's screen-privacy change, and this is the first moment the child home is what anyone can see (HUNT6-I-4)" (apps/mobile/src/lib/app-session.ts:100-102), and "the two callers that KNOW the app is in the foreground settle it: the 'active' handler in src/lib/app-session.ts" (apps/mobile/src/lib/mode.ts:143-146).
findings.mechanism: Round 6 moved `setScreenPrivacy(false)` out of `lockParentAreaOnDevice` and replaced it with a module-level debt flag (apps/mobile/src/lib/mode.ts:206, `childSpaceOwedScreenPrivacyOff = true`), to be applied later by `settleChildSpaceScreenPrivacy` (mode.ts:161-167). The background handler reaches that assignment only after three awaited SecureStore round-trips: `readMode()` (apps/mobile/src/lib/app-session.ts:111 -> `currentMode`, mode.ts:374-376, an awaited `storage.getItem`), then inside `lockParentAreaOnDevice` an awaited `storage.getItem(childRefreshToken)` (mode.ts:192-195) and an awaited `storage.setItem(mode,'child')` (mode.ts:197). The new 'active' branch (app-session.ts:99-104) is synchronous in the AppState handler and returns immediately. So on a quick background/foreground cycle — the app switcher, the notification shade, a dismissed call, on Android a plain onPause/onResume pair — 'active' fires while that promise chain is still pending, `settleChildSpaceScreenPrivacy` reads `childSpaceOwedScreenPrivacyOff === false` (mode.ts:164) and returns without doing anything; the chain then sets the flag to true. The app is now in the foreground, mode is 'child', `resetNavigationToChildHome()` has run, and OS capture protection is still ON from `enterParentMode` (mode.ts:295). Nothing else can clear it: `useChildModeOnFocus` (apps/mobile/src/family/ui.tsx:391-398) returns early because the mode it reads is already 'child', and the only other settler is the Lock button's own chain (ui.tsx:374-378), which this path never runs. Before the change, `lockParentAreaOnDevice` applied `setScreenPrivacy(false)` itself, so the outcome did not depend on event ordering.
findings.impact: The child is handed back a tablet whose own space silently refuses screenshots, screen recording and casting until the app is backgrounded and foregrounded again — exactly MOB-R2-05 / BUG-287 / HUNT5-G-4, the defect round 5 fixed. On Android FLAG_SECURE also blocks casting the whole screen, so a parent trying to mirror the child's homework to a TV sees a black frame with no explanation. It also leaves a stale debt behind, which is the precondition for HUNT7-A-2.
findings.ruled_out: (1) That some other path re-applies it: I enumerated every `setScreenPrivacy` caller (`grep -rn setScreenPrivacy apps/mobile/src apps/mobile/app`) — mode.ts:166 (settle), :261 (signOutParent), :295 (enterParentMode), :332 (enterChildMode), and the effect impl at runtime.ts:157. On this path none runs: the mode is 'child' so `useChildModeOnFocus`/`enterChildMode` return early (ui.tsx:393-395), and no sign-out or parent-mode entry happens. (2) That the flag might be set before the event: it is assigned at mode.ts:206, strictly after three awaits, so any 'active' delivered inside that window loses the race — this is not a hypothetical interleaving, it is the ordinary one for a sub-100ms foreground return. (3) That the app might be killed instead, making the flag irrelevant: that is a different case and mode.ts:135-137 already covers it (a fresh process starts with capture allowed). (4) That a test already covers it: the new case in apps/mobile/src/lib/app-session.test.ts:262-283 does `fake.appStateListener?.('background'); await settle();` before firing 'active', i.e. it always awaits the lock first, so it cannot see this ordering. (5) That 'active' might not fire on a short cycle: it is the only foreground event React Native delivers on Android, and on iOS the sequence is 'inactive' then 'active', so 'active' still arrives.
findings.reproduction: apps/mobile/src/lib/app-session.test.ts, alongside '[repro] backgrounding a paired tablet keeps adult screen privacy on until the app is active': fire `fake.appStateListener?.('background')` and `fake.appStateListener?.('active')` back to back with no `await settle()` between them, then `await settle()` and assert `expect(fake.privacy).toEqual([false])`. Today it is `[]`, and `childSpaceOwesScreenPrivacy()` is still true.
findings.suggested_fix: Do not make the child space's privacy change depend on an event that may already have passed. Either settle it at the end of the lock itself when the caller knows the app is foreground (pass that fact in, so the backgrounding caller does not), or, if the debt is kept, have the background chain re-check after setting it — e.g. `lockParentAreaOnDevice` returns whether a debt was recorded and the app-session handler settles it when AppState.currentState is 'active' at that moment. Keep the HUNT6-I-4 property: nothing may turn protection off while the app is leaving the foreground.

findings.title: The screen-privacy debt is never scoped to the child space nor cleared on re-entering parent mode, so a stale debt turns adult screen privacy OFF while the parent area is on screen
findings.claim_under_review: "Settles that debt — and only from a caller that is sure the app is in the foreground, since the whole point is that the adult frame stays protected while the OS snapshots it" (apps/mobile/src/lib/mode.ts:156-160), and "A background lock must not switch adult screen privacy OFF; that is the state the next adult depends on" (HUNT6-I-4's lead decision, docs/hardening/round6-fix-plan.json).
findings.mechanism: `settleChildSpaceScreenPrivacy` (apps/mobile/src/lib/mode.ts:161-167) applies `setScreenPrivacy(false)` on the sole condition that the flag is set. It does not read the current mode, and no other function clears the flag: `enterParentMode` writes mode 'parent' and `setScreenPrivacy(true)` (mode.ts:294-295) and leaves `childSpaceOwedScreenPrivacyOff` untouched; so do `enterChildMode` (mode.ts:326-332) and `signOutParent` (mode.ts:330-332). The app-session handler then calls it on EVERY 'active' transition regardless of mode (apps/mobile/src/lib/app-session.ts:99-104), and on iOS 'active' arrives after any 'inactive' blip that never reached 'background' — control centre, notification shade, a Face ID or permission dialog, a dismissed call — none of which runs the lock. So once a debt outlives a return to parent mode, the next such blip strips adult protection while parent screens are mounted. Two ways to get that stale debt: (a) HUNT7-A-1's ordering race leaves the flag set with no settle; (b) the Lock button chain (apps/mobile/src/family/ui.tsx:374-378) sets the flag at mode.ts:206 and only settles after `await effects.relockOnServer()` (mode.ts:210, a network POST), so a parent who locks and PINs back in before that call returns gets `setScreenPrivacy(false)` delivered into parent mode. The harm then composes with the very leak HUNT6-I-4 fixed: with protection off in parent mode, the next backgrounding runs the lock, which no longer turns protection on, and the OS snapshots the still-painted ADULT frame for its app-switcher card (`resetNavigationToChildHome` is a JS `router.replace`, runtime.ts:145, which cannot paint while suspended).
findings.impact: Whoever picks the tablet up next — in a family product that is the child — can screenshot, screen-record or cast the parent area, and sees the adult frame in the app-switcher card: the family name, the children's nicknames and grades, the planner and the billing screen. That is the state MOB-R2-01 and HUNT6-I-4 exist to protect, reproduced by the fix written for it.
findings.ruled_out: (1) That some caller clears the debt on leaving the child space: I read every writer of the flag — mode.ts:206 sets it, mode.ts:165 clears it, and nothing else assigns it (`grep -n childSpaceOwedScreenPrivacyOff apps/mobile/src/lib/mode.ts` gives 148, 152, 164, 165, 206). `enterParentMode` does not. (2) That the settle might be harmless in parent mode because something re-asserts protection: the only `setScreenPrivacy(true)` is in `enterParentMode` (mode.ts:295), which has already run by then; no focus effect or screen re-applies it (`grep -rn setScreenPrivacy apps/mobile`). (3) That 'active' only follows 'background', which would mean the lock always ran first: React Native delivers 'inactive' -> 'active' on iOS for non-backgrounding interruptions, and app-session.ts:99 matches 'active' with no guard on what preceded it. (4) That the Lock-button path is not reachable because the relock is fast: it is an authenticated POST through `stepUpApi()`/`lockParentArea` (runtime.ts:153-155) with the client's default timeout, so on a slow link it can outlast a 6-digit PIN entry plus an unlock POST; I am not resting the finding on that path alone, which is why (a) is named first. (5) That an existing test covers it: apps/mobile/src/lib/mode-r2.review.test.ts:244-255 settles immediately after the lock and its afterEach (mode-r2.review.test.ts:68-73) drains the flag between cases, so no case ever holds a debt across an `enterParentMode`.
findings.reproduction: apps/mobile/src/lib/mode-r2.review.test.ts, in the 'locking a paired family tablet returns it to the child space' describe: after `await lockParentAreaOnDevice(storage, effects())` (debt set), call `await enterParentMode(storage, effects(), { unlocked: true, unlockedUntil: SERVER_UNTIL, unlockSeconds: UNLOCK_SECONDS }, SERVER_NOW)`, then `const fx = effects(); await settleChildSpaceScreenPrivacy(fx); expect(fx.calls).not.toContain('privacy:false')`. Today `fx.calls` is `['privacy:false']`.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the debt name what it is owed for and check it at settle time: record it with the mode/space it belongs to and have `settleChildSpaceScreenPrivacy` re-read `currentMode(storage)` and do nothing unless the device is still in child mode; and clear the flag in `enterParentMode` (and in `signOutParent`/`enterChildMode`, which apply the privacy state themselves) so no settle can arrive after the state it was computed for has changed. Do not remove the HUNT6-I-4 deferral itself — the adult frame must stay protected while the app is leaving the foreground.

findings.title: The reversal's headline property — "a captured request body is worthless once its token has been rotated" — is false: such a body is a repeatable remote kill switch for the child's live session, and the owner's sign-off record states the false version
findings.claim_under_review: "a captured body is worthless again ONCE THE TOKEN IN IT HAS BEEN ROTATED — the property the recovery sold, and the only one it took away" (apps/api/src/routes/child-auth.ts:260-262); "a captured refresh request body must buy an attacker nothing ONCE THE TOKEN IN IT HAS BEEN ROTATED" (apps/api/tests/mobile-r2.review.test.ts:286-288); "What we are keeping is the property a logged request body needs: after its rotation it is worthless" (docs/Owner_Actions.md:55, owner action #45); "a request body captured after its rotation is worthless again, which is the property a logged body needs" (docs/Bug_Ledger.md:251); "in exchange for a captured refresh body being worthless once its token has rotated" (docs/Requirement_Coverage.md:17).
findings.mechanism: Presenting a rotated token is not inert, it is an action. `POST /v1/child/refresh` finds the row, sees `row.used_at`, and unconditionally (a) revokes the child's live session — `update public.child_sessions set revoked_at = ..., revoke_reason = 'refresh_token_reuse'` (apps/api/src/routes/child-auth.ts:274), (b) inserts an `audit_events` row (child-auth.ts:275-278), and (c) revokes the device row so the parent's list stops showing it connected (child-auth.ts:281, `stampDeviceWhenNoLiveSession`). Nothing authenticates the presenter and nothing bounds this beyond `childRefreshPerNetwork` = 240/hour (apps/api/src/middleware/rate-limit.ts:124); the per-session rule is only reached on the success path (child-auth.ts:290-295), so a replayer never spends it. The token row survives as long as the session does and for `SESSION_ROW_RETENTION_DAYS` = 30 after it ends (apps/api/src/auth/housekeeping.ts:22; migration 0850 states the rule: "a live session keeps all of its tokens, however old: a used token presented again is how rotation detects theft"), so the window is the whole life of the session, not a moment. The audit insert has no `and revoked_at is null` guard, so each further replay appends another row to a table family.ts:37 records as one that "nothing prunes". The same tree contradicts the claim in its own threat model: docs/Threat_Model.md:46 names T20 as "Child session revoked by token replay", and the two mitigations it offers (one session layer, single-flight refresh) address only the device's own second refresher, not an external replayer. The existing green case at apps/api/tests/mobile-r2.review.test.ts:341-364 ('a rotated token presented seconds later is theft, and its replacement dies with it') is itself the demonstration: a body whose token has been rotated ends the session.
findings.impact: An attacker holding one captured refresh body can unpair a named child's tablet on demand, repeatedly, for the life of that session: the child is told to ask a grown-up to connect the device again, and the parent has to complete a PIN step-up and mint and re-enter a new pairing code (`assertRecentUnlock` on POST /children/:childId/pairing-code, apps/api/src/routes/family.ts:398). The owner is being asked, in docs/Owner_Actions.md #45, to accept BUG-244 on the stated basis that a logged body is worthless afterwards — the one security property the reversal was sold on — and that basis is wrong in the direction that makes the residual look smaller, which is the exact failure round 6 exists to correct (BUG-294/L-058).
findings.ruled_out: (1) That the capability is new: it is not — `git diff 1cfebcc 5ba16c3 -- apps/api/src/routes/child-auth.ts` shows the `row.used_at` body is byte-identical to pre-BUG-244 and only the comment changed. What is new is the claim, written in this diff at child-auth.ts:260-262 and mobile-r2.review.test.ts:286-288 and copied into the owner's sign-off. I am filing the claim, not a code regression. (2) That the row might be gone by the time a body is replayed, making it a no-op 401: migration 0850's retention rule keeps every token of a LIVE session (supabase/migrations/0850_hardening_r1_db2.sql:108-116) and prunes only 30 days after the session ended, so for a live session the row is always there. (3) That the revoke might not commit on a 401: the branch returns `{ kind: 'reused' }` (child-auth.ts:282) rather than throwing, so `deps.db.asService` commits before the route raises UNAUTHENTICATED. (4) That a rate limit makes it a single shot: only the per-network rule (240/hour) runs before the body is parsed; the per-session rule is after the reuse branch. (5) That the claim might be defensible as "buys no ACCESS": the sentences say "worthless" and "buy an attacker nothing", unqualified, and Owner_Actions #45 offers it as "the property a logged request body needs". (6) I checked that the capture premise is not itself supported in-tree, which makes the over-claim worse rather than better: the API logs no bodies (apps/api/src/app.ts:66-73 logs event/requestId/status/durationMs only), so "a logged request body is the realistic capture vector" (child-auth.ts:255-256) is a hypothesis about a proxy or middlebox, not about this service. (7) That a parent is told the false thing directly: they are not — no route or screen reads `revoke_reason` or `audit_events` (`grep -rn 'revoke_reason|audit_events' apps/*/src` returns writes only), which is why I have not filed this high.
findings.reproduction: apps/api/tests/mobile-r2.review.test.ts, in the 'the refresh request carries no recovery id at all (BUG-244 reopened, HUNT6-A-1)' describe: pair a device, rotate once, then replay the ORIGINAL body from a different `cf-connecting-ip` and assert what the docstring claims — `expect((await sessionRow(device.fam.familyId, label)).revoke_reason).toBeNull()`. It fails: the reason is 'refresh_token_reuse'. The already-green case at mobile-r2.review.test.ts:341 is the same demonstration inside the same file as the claim at line 287.
findings.suggested_fix: Say what is true, in all five places, and keep the code as it is: a body captured after its token has been rotated can no longer obtain tokens (which is the real gain over the recovery), but it remains a presentation that ends that child's session — so a replayer who has one can unpair the tablet at will for the life of the session and for the 30-day token retention after it, once per request up to the per-network limit, appending an audit row each time. State that as the residual the owner is accepting in docs/Owner_Actions.md #45, add it to T20 in docs/Threat_Model.md next to the threat title that already names it, and pin it with the assertion in the reproduction above (inverted to assert the revoke, so the record and the test agree). Separately consider guarding the audit insert with `and revoked_at is null` semantics so a replay loop cannot append to an unpruned table indefinitely — do not weaken the revoke itself.

findings.title: The reuse guard's new premise sentence ("a second presentation means two parties hold it") is false and is contradicted three lines later in the same comment, and "an unpairing a parent can undo in one tap" contradicts "the parent has to mint a new pairing code"
findings.claim_under_review: "Rotation is the only way a token becomes used, so a second presentation means two parties hold it" (apps/api/src/routes/child-auth.ts:241-243), and "the feature only avoided an occasional unpairing a parent can undo in one tap" (child-auth.ts:266-268).
findings.mechanism: The guard is `if (row.used_at)` (apps/api/src/routes/child-auth.ts:239). What it establishes is the adjacent fact — this token has been rotated before — not the fact the comment claims. One party presenting the same token twice satisfies it exactly: that is BUG-244, and the same comment admits it at child-auth.ts:246-248 ("this also fires when a rotation's response is lost on the way back to the tablet"). The counterexample is a green test in the tree with one party and no attacker: apps/mobile/src/family/child-session-r2.review.test.ts:398-420, '[repro] a retry after a lost answer presents the spent token, and the tablet is unpaired', whose mock server rotates then drops the answer, after which the single device presents the spent token again. The second sentence is wrong on the product: minting a new pairing code needs a PIN step-up (`assertRecentUnlock`, apps/api/src/routes/family.ts:398), a parent-area navigation, the code request, then 'Use a different code' and an 8-symbol entry on the tablet — which is what the same comment says at child-auth.ts:247-248 and what apps/mobile/src/family/child-session.ts:156-157 and docs/Owner_Actions.md:55 say too.
findings.impact: This comment is the only statement of the rule at the point of enforcement, and the round-6 process change (docs/hardening/round6-fix-plan.json: "state its premise in one sentence and say what observable fact establishes it") makes it load-bearing for the next reviewer. As written it tells them the guard proves theft, which is the belief that made BUG-244 ship in the first place; and 'one tap' understates the cost of the accepted defect in the same paragraph that justifies accepting it.
findings.ruled_out: (1) That the sentence is a fair shorthand: it is stated as an inference ("so"), and the branch's whole difficulty is that the inference does not hold, which the next paragraph concedes. L-053 applies and the code is the TRUE side: revoking on any re-presentation is the right rule, so the comment is what must change. (2) That 'in one tap' might refer to something else, e.g. a device list action: I checked the parent surfaces — apps/mobile/app/(parent)/children.tsx and the devices screen offer 'Disconnect', not 'reconnect'; there is no one-tap re-pair, and POST /children/:childId/pairing-code requires a fresh unlock. (3) That the removal itself is wrong: it is not, and I am not asking for any behaviour change here. (4) That another file already states it correctly, making this harmless: apps/api/tests/auth.test.ts:153-158 and packages/contracts/src/auth.ts:52-66 both state the rule without the false inference, which is why the disagreement is worth resolving rather than leaving two records.
findings.reproduction: apps/mobile/src/family/child-session-r2.review.test.ts:398 ('[repro] a retry after a lost answer presents the spent token, and the tablet is unpaired') passes today with exactly one party presenting the token twice, which is the counterexample to child-auth.ts:241-243; no new test is needed to show the comment false, and no assertion can be written that makes the sentence true.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the inference with the fact the guard has: this token has already been rotated, so it must not be served again — a second presentation is EITHER a second holder OR the rightful holder retrying after a lost response, and because the server cannot tell them apart it fails closed and revokes, which is what makes BUG-244 the accepted cost recorded below. And replace 'undo in one tap' with what the same comment already says two paragraphs up: the parent completes a PIN step-up, mints a new pairing code and re-enters it on the tablet.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The server's `row.used_at` branch is back to pre-BUG-244 behaviour: every presentation of a rotated token revokes, audits and stamps the device, with no path that returns 200 or tokens.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Diffed the whole route against the last pre-BUG-244 blob rather than reading it: `git show 1cfebcc:apps/api/src/routes/child-auth.ts` vs `git show 5ba16c3:...` — the only differences in the entire file are comment blocks. Then walked every exit of the refresh handler at 5ba16c3 for a path that could skip a write: `!row` -> invalid (child-auth.ts:229); `row.used_at` -> revoke (274) + audit (275-278) + stamp (281) + `{kind:'reused'}` (282); `!row.live` -> stamp + invalid (285-289); `!consented()` -> invalid (290); success -> rotate (297-298). Checked that the reuse branch returns rather than throws, so `deps.db.asService` commits the revoke before the 401; checked the revoke is not gated on `row.live`, so an expired-token replay still ends a live session; checked `for update of t` serialises two concurrent presentations of one token so the second re-reads `used_at` and revokes.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: No branch returns tokens or a 2xx from the used_at path, none skips the audit insert or the device stamp, and the transaction commits. The only thing I could find to say about the branch is that its audit insert is unguarded on repeat replays, which is folded into HUNT7-A-3.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The contract is closed: a body carrying `refreshRequestId` is a 400, and no second parse, passthrough, `.partial()`, union arm or middleware can accept it.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Read `childRefreshRequestSchema` at packages/contracts/src/auth.ts:67-69 (a `z.strictObject` with `refreshToken` only). Grepped every reference to the schema across apps and packages — exactly one production parse, apps/api/src/routes/child-auth.ts:205. Read `readJson` (apps/api/src/app.ts:187-203): `schema.safeParse` then `ApiError('VALIDATION_FAILED')`, mapped to 400 by packages/contracts/src/errors.ts:41. Enumerated every middleware registered on `*` in apps/api/src/app.ts: the request/CORS wrapper (40) and `bodyLimit` (77-85) — no body validator, no `zValidator`, nothing that re-parses or strips. Grepped every caller of `/v1/child/refresh` in apps and packages: the device (apps/mobile/src/family/child-session.ts:159-164) and tests only. Checked there is no partial/passthrough/extend/union derived from the schema anywhere.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: One strict schema, one parse, one 400, and no other surface reaches the route. The existing case at apps/api/tests/mobile-r2.review.test.ts:308-326 also goes red if the field is re-added, so the closure is pinned and not merely asserted.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: Nothing on the device reads or is affected by the `pl.child.refresh.rid` key that a round-5 build wrote and that this diff does not delete.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Grepped apps, packages, supabase, scripts and .github for `refresh.rid`, `childRefreshRequestId`, `parseStoredRequest` and `pendingRequest` — the only survivors are two test assertions of ABSENCE. Read `secureStorage` (apps/mobile/src/lib/secure-storage.ts): a thin get/set/delete over expo-secure-store with no key enumeration, so nothing iterates the keychain. Read `unpairChildDevice` (mode.ts:366-372): it now deletes only the two child keys, so the stale record would survive 'Disconnect' and account closure on an upgraded device. Then tested the premise that such a device exists: docs/Connections.md records Expo/EAS as **Blocked** ('native builds and installs cannot be produced here') and every Supabase, RevenueCat, Amazon and Cloudflare row as blocked, and `git ls-files apps/mobile/dist` is empty, so the local Expo web export is untracked. Also checked the opposite direction — a round-5 client talking to the round-6 API would now get a 400 on every refresh and, because 400 is VALIDATION_FAILED rather than UNAUTHENTICATED (child-session.ts:169), would throw forever rather than unpair — which is only unreachable for the same reason.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: No code path reads the key, nothing enumerates keychain keys, and no build has ever been installed on a device, so no keychain anywhere holds it. The one thing I would flag to the lead rather than file: the new case 'unpairing leaves nothing of the child in the keychain' (child-session-r2.review.test.ts:471-478) seeds only the two current keys, so its name would be false for an upgraded device — true today only because of the no-deployment premise, which is the same premise migration 0880's deletion rests on. If a build ever ships before that premise changes, `unpairChildDevice` should delete the legacy key once.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: Deleting migration 0880 from the tree, rather than dropping the column in a later migration, breaks nothing that assumes 0880 exists or that the sequence has no gap.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Read the deleted file (`git show b802686:supabase/migrations/0880_child_refresh_idempotency.sql`): it only adds `used_request_id`, a partial index and a column comment, all `if not exists`. Read the loader: `listMigrations` is `readdir(...).filter(.sql).sort()` (supabase/scripts/migrate.ts:9-12) and `applyMigrations` iterates it — no manifest, no checksum, no count, no contiguity check. Read supabase/tests/harness.ts: a fresh `create database pl_test_<random>` per test file, so no local database can carry a stale column into the new negative assertions. Grepped scripts/, .github/workflows/ and supabase/tests/ for any migration count, order or numbering assertion — none; `PL_MIGRATIONS_ONLY` is a prefix filter, not a sequence check. Listed the directory: 0870 then 0890, a real gap, and checked docs/Deployment_Runbook.md:70-74, which tells the operator to `list supabase/migrations` rather than naming a fixed set, and :647-648, whose forward-only rule bites only for an APPLIED file. Tested that premise: docs/Connections.md says no Supabase project has ever been connected and Owner_Actions #3/#21 are still open, so no database has the column.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Ordering is purely lexicographic over whatever files are present, nothing counts or checksums them, every test database is created fresh, and the 'never edit an applied file' rule is not violated because the file was never applied anywhere. The gap is real but inert. The new DB assertion (supabase/tests/hardening_r1_db2.test.ts:534-547) is also a genuine repro — it would have failed at b802686 — and it carries a live mutation anchor, the arrayContaining over the real columns, so the two negatives cannot pass on an empty result from a renamed table.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: Each surviving test in the reversal can tell the two worlds apart: it goes red if the recovery is re-added.

findings.title: The stage BUDGET bounds EVERY later attempt, not only the raised truncation retry, so the split silently bought each astra stage an extra billed attempt after a timeout — while routing.ts and the owner's cost record both say the budget is "not money"
findings.claim_under_review: routing.ts:292-294: "These are HOLDS, not spend: settleSpend replaces each with the actual usage, so a call that succeeds costs no more than before and the exposure is a family near their monthly ceiling waiting a tick longer." (repeated in docs/Cost_Analysis.md:120-121: "and every one of them settles to metered usage, so these are reservations and not money")
findings.mechanism: packages/ai/src/run.ts:273-280 selects the cost bound on `attempt === 1` ALONE — `canAttempt(attempt === 1 ? limits : { ...limits, maxCostMicros: maxStageCostMicros }, …)`. There is no `budgetRaised` condition, so the larger number governs the cumulative-cost check for EVERY attempt after the first, whatever ended the first one. An attempt whose usage the provider never reported (a client-side timeout or a 5xx) is deliberately metered at the FULL upper bound it was admitted with (run.ts:299-315 with `usageUnknown`, run.ts:185-187), so `spent` after such a failure equals the admission estimate exactly. Coaching (astra: 10 micros/input token, 50/output token, B=2,500, maxAttempts 2) is therefore admitted on attempt 1 while 10E + 125,000 <= 300,000 (E <= 17,500), and attempt 2 is now allowed while 2 x (10E + 125,000) <= 407,520, i.e. E <= 7,876. At b802686 the same comparison used the single 300,000 number (git show b802686:packages/ai/src/routing.ts:203 and the pre-diff `canAttempt(args.limits, …)`), i.e. E <= 2,500. Coaching's floor input is 1,626 tokens (routing.ts:120) and its production envelope adds the printed question and the child's answer (scan-process.ts:1940-1951; schemas admit up to 4,000 bytes each), so ordinary coaching requests sit squarely in the newly-opened 2,501..7,876 band — including the "long worksheet question" the round's own case in apps/api/tests/jobs-r2.review.test.ts uses. Same arithmetic: daily_set 2,500 -> 9,162; thursday_bundle 5,000 -> 16,680; semantic_check 5,200 -> 5,400. In that band the stage now makes and pays for a SECOND astra generation where the old number stopped it after one. That is real spend, not a reservation, and it is the same defect BUG-312/HUNT6-D-4 closed one docstring higher up in the same file (routing.ts:67-78 correctly qualifies EXTRACTION_GRADING_COST_MICROS; routing.ts:292-294 does not qualify the new budget table at all).
findings.impact: The owner pays for one extra astra generation (up to ~0.20 USD for coaching, ~0.24 for daily_set, ~0.47 for thursday_bundle) on every transient-failure path in that input band, and the two documents they would read to understand the round-6 change — the constant's own docstring and docs/Cost_Analysis.md section 3 — tell them the change moves no money. The behaviour itself may well be what the lead wants (a second try means a child gets a hint instead of a template fallback), but it was neither reported nor priced: the lead's own instruction for HUNT6-D-1 was "REPORT the new per-stage numbers and the new worst-case hold", and the failure-path arm was not in the report.
findings.ruled_out: (a) Not a ceiling breach: the hold reserves the same budget (scan-process.ts:1232, learning-jobs.ts:678) and runStage's cumulative check bounds metered spend by it, so recorded spend never passes the hold — I checked both hold sites and the group sum (grading 216,816 + verification 100,000 = 316,816, exactly what `spending(['grading','verification'])` reserves). (b) Not pre-existing: git show b802686:packages/ai/src/routing.ts shows coaching/followup/daily_set/thursday_bundle/semantic_check at the identical caps, and the pre-diff `raisedOutputBudget`/loop both used `limits.maxCostMicros`, so at b802686 the whole stage was bounded by 300,000. The round-6 routing.ts diff changes no limit VALUE — only the added budget table widens the cumulative bound. (c) Not confined to truncation: I traced every branch that reaches `attempt += 1` — a retryable provider error (run.ts:337-350), a non-max_output_tokens incomplete (run.ts:385-387) and a validation rejection (run.ts:400-401) all continue the loop with `maxOutputTokens` unchanged, and all are weighed against the budget. (d) Not caught by a test: run-metering.test.ts's "timed-out attempts count against the stage budget" case uses extraction, whose two numbers are the same 216,816, so it cannot observe the widening; no case drives an astra stage with a 5xx. (e) run.ts's own loop comment (run.ts:267-272) does say "Every LATER attempt is weighed against the budget", so the code comment there is accurate — it is routing.ts:292-294 and the doc that are false, which is why this is filed against the constant and not the loop.
findings.reproduction: New case in packages/ai/src/run-truncation.test.ts (or run-metering.test.ts): `runStage` for `PROMPTS.coaching` with `limits: PROPOSED_STAGE_LIMITS.coaching`, `estimatedInputTokens: 5_000`, and a mock client that always answers `{ kind: 'error', status: 503, retryable: true, timedOut: false }`. Today: `out.attempts` has length 2 and `out.attempts.reduce((n,a)=>n+a.costMicros,0)` is 350,000. `expect(total).toBeLessThanOrEqual(PROPOSED_STAGE_LIMITS.coaching.maxCostMicros)` — the property routing.ts:292-294 asserts — is RED at 350,000 > 300,000, and would have been green at b802686 (one attempt, 175,000).
findings.suggested_fix: Decide which of the two is true (L-053). Either (1) keep the code and make the prose honest: replace routing.ts:292-294 with a paragraph that says the budget is ALSO the cumulative-cost bound for every attempt after the first, name the band per stage at which a timed-out or 5xx attempt now gets a second billed generation where the admission cap used to stop it, and put the same two lines in docs/Cost_Analysis.md section 3 beside the hold table — plus the regression case above so the band is checkable; or (2) keep the prose and narrow the code: weigh a later attempt against `limits.maxCostMicros` unless `budgetRaised` is true, so only the one raised retry draws on the budget. Do not simply lower a budget below its ceiling — that reopens BUG-309.

findings.title: The owner's new worst-case-hold table omits the thursday_bundle personalization hold and states the largest single hold is 483,240 micro-USD when the same code path reserves 933,600
findings.claim_under_review: docs/Cost_Analysis.md:130: "The largest single hold a family can hit is the personalization stage at 483,240 micro-USD ($0.48)." and the hold table at :124-128, whose only personalization row is "| Practice personalization | daily_set | 483,240 | $0.483240 |"
findings.mechanism: `personalizeItems` takes the hold with `acquireSpendHold(deps, PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS[stage])` (apps/api/src/jobs/learning-jobs.ts:678) and its `stage` parameter is `'daily_set' | 'thursday_bundle'` (learning-jobs.ts:628). The thursday arm is a live production path: `generateThursdayReview` is registered as the `thursday_review_generate` handler (learning-jobs.ts:1429, 1434), is enqueued by the tick (learning-jobs.ts:1641), and calls `personalizeItems(..., 'thursday_bundle', ...)` at learning-jobs.ts:1234-1240. `PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS.thursday_bundle` is 933,600 (packages/ai/src/routing.ts:315), so the hold that path takes is 933,600 micro-USD ($0.93) — 93% larger than the figure the record names as the maximum, and larger than every row in the table. The same understatement is in the round-6 comment the doc was written from: learning-jobs.ts:670-676 illustrates the fix with "daily_set's cap is 350,000 micros and its two attempts may cost 483,240" and routing.ts:270-272 says the budget is what "learning-jobs.ts reserves … for the personalization stage", singular, while there are two personalization stages with budgets 483,240 and 933,600.
findings.impact: The figure exists so the owner can size the monthly spend ceiling (`public.spend_budgets`) against the peak reservation; it is understated by 450,360 micro-USD. A ceiling set with $0.48 of headroom in mind refuses the Thursday review bundle at `acquireSpendHold` and the child silently receives the un-personalized bank items (learning-jobs.ts:679-684 returns `unchanged` on SpendCeilingReached) — and the record the owner would consult to diagnose that says no such hold exists.
findings.ruled_out: (a) Not a stale row from before the split: the whole section is new in the round-6 records commit 2ce8eb8 (git diff 5ba16c3 HEAD -- docs/Cost_Analysis.md, +50 lines), written from the fixer's report under the lead's instruction "REPORT … the new worst-case hold for the lead to record in docs/Cost_Analysis.md". (b) thursday_bundle is not dead code or flag-gated off: the handler is in the learning handler map and the tick enqueues it whenever `handlers.daily_set_generate` is registered (dispatcher.ts:1317, learning-jobs.ts:1428-1435). (c) The hold is not nested inside a larger one that would already cover it — `personalizeItems` takes its own hold and settles it in a `finally` (learning-jobs.ts:678, 731-734); there is no enclosing `spending()`. (d) Not merely a bigger number than needed: the budget really is what the stage may spend (thursday_bundle's full-raise ceiling is 933,600, which I re-derived: 16,800 + 300,000 + 16,800 + 600,000), so the row is missing, not wrong in the code. (e) 933,600 is inside the safe-integer range `evaluateSpend` requires, so no other guard hides it.
findings.reproduction: apps/api/tests/learning-jobs.test.ts: a thursday_bundle twin of "the personalization hold reserves the stage BUDGET the raised retry can spend (F-HOLD)" — `personalizeItems(..., 'thursday_bundle', ...)` with the same always-truncated client and `expect(heldWhileRunning).toBe(BigInt(PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS.thursday_bundle))`, plus `expect(PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS.thursday_bundle).toBeGreaterThan(PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS.daily_set)`. That second assertion alone contradicts the doc sentence.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the missing row to docs/Cost_Analysis.md's hold table ("| Thursday review personalization | thursday_bundle | 933,600 | $0.933600 |") and correct :130 to name thursday_bundle at 933,600 as the largest single hold. Make routing.ts:270-272 say "for EITHER personalization stage (daily_set 483,240, thursday_bundle 933,600)" and add the thursday figure to the learning-jobs.ts:670-676 comment so the doc cannot be re-derived from a one-stage example again. Add the thursday_bundle hold case so the number is pinned by a test rather than by prose.

findings.title: The dispatcher's rewritten "that bounds the LEDGER … that is the whole guarantee" claim rests on a declared worst case the scan pipeline's own timeouts already exceed with a single coached question
findings.claim_under_review: apps/api/src/jobs/dispatcher.ts:1330-1331: "The LEDGER alone cannot starve it: no job is claimed that would run past TICK_WALL_LIMIT_MS − TICK_TRAILING_RESERVE_MS (R4-JOBS-4). That is the whole guarantee" and dispatcher.ts:748-751: "never into its last TICK_TRAILING_RESERVE_MS (R4-JOBS-4). That bounds the LEDGER"
findings.mechanism: The claim filter compares a STATIC per-kind declaration, not the run: `(JOB_WORST_CASE_MS[kind] ?? DEFAULT_JOB_WORST_CASE_MS) <= remaining` (dispatcher.ts:752-755), with `JOB_WORST_CASE_MS = { scan_process: 7 * 60_000 }` (dispatcher.ts:115). Nothing enforces that declaration afterwards: `runOne` awaits the handler with no deadline (dispatcher.ts:771-779) and scan-process.ts has no wall-clock check — its only early exit is `pause()` at the spend ceiling (scan-process.ts:1002). The declaration is already below the scan's own declared worst case, from the constants in packages/ai/src/routing.ts:173-212: extraction 3 attempts x 45,000 ms + grading 3 x 45,000 + verification 2 x 45,000 = 360,000 ms, plus coaching's 2 x 45,000 ms per coached question (scan-process.ts:1845 calls `coach` once per graded question, with no cap on how many). One coached question is therefore 450,000 ms > 420,000 ms, and the constant's own docstring (dispatcher.ts:111-114) describes exactly that shape: "extraction, grading and verification plus up to two 45-second coaching calls per wrong answer". A ten-question worksheet all wrong declares 1,260,000 ms — past the whole 900,000 ms invocation. So the round-6 rewrite strengthened a sentence about what the ledger DOES to a guarantee the filter cannot make: it bounds the declared estimate, which is a fact adjacent to "no job runs past the wall".
findings.impact: A scan claimed at minute 6 of a 15-minute invocation (the filter's limit for a 7-minute declaration) can still be killed at the wall mid-run. That spends a job attempt, leaves the row `running` with a 20-minute lease so no later tick can recover it (dispatcher.ts:717-722 recovers only expired leases), and the parent's assignment sits in `checking`/`verifying` for up to twenty minutes before anything retries. The trailing entitlement sweep gets nothing on that tick too — the residual BUG-264 the same comment says "carries" — but the comment now tells the next reader the ledger cannot cause it, which is the wrong place to stop looking.
findings.ruled_out: (a) There is no runtime deadline I missed: I grepped dispatcher.ts and scan-process.ts for deadline/budget checks — `JobDeferral` exists but scan-process returns one only from `pause()` (the spend ceiling), never from a clock check, and `runOne` has no timeout around `handler(deps, job)`. (b) 7 minutes is not a measured p95 that supersedes the declared timeouts: it is a hypothesis constant beside the caps routing.ts marks "PROPOSED … hypotheses to replace with measured p95", and the worst case is precisely what the constant exists to express. (c) The coaching loop is not capped: scan-process.ts:1823-1846 iterates every graded question and there is no MAX_COACHED constant anywhere in the file. (d) A recheck run skips extraction (scan-process.ts:1320-1327 `hasQuestions`), but even 135,000 + 90,000 + 90,000 = 315,000 ms plus two coached questions exceeds 420,000 ms. (e) Not already filed: the round-6 findings for this area are HUNT6-D-2 and HUNT6-D-3, both about the trailing-slice prose and the entitlement-sync example; neither touches JOB_WORST_CASE_MS, and BUG-200/BUG-238 introduced the constant without pricing it.
findings.reproduction: apps/api/tests/jobs-r2.review.test.ts, beside the existing claim-budget cases: derive the scan's declared worst case from the production constants — `PROPOSED_STAGE_LIMITS.extraction.maxAttempts * timeoutMs + grading… + verification… + coaching.maxAttempts * coaching.timeoutMs` — and assert it is <= the declared `JOB_WORST_CASE_MS.scan_process`. Red today: 450,000 > 420,000 (requires exporting JOB_WORST_CASE_MS, or a small exported helper, from dispatcher.ts).
findings.suggested_fix: Decide which of the two is true. Either raise `JOB_WORST_CASE_MS.scan_process` to a number the pipeline's own timeouts and attempt counts justify (and say in its docstring that it is derived from PROPOSED_STAGE_LIMITS, with the test above pinning the derivation), or keep 7 minutes and downgrade the two comments to what the filter really establishes — that no job whose DECLARED worst case exceeds the remaining time is claimed, that nothing enforces the declaration at run time, and that a scan with several coached questions can still reach the wall. Do not weaken the claim filter.

findings.title: "Every `maxCostMicros` here is an ADMISSION bound and nothing else: the largest single request the stage may send" is enforced on attempt 1 only, and followup's configured pair allows a single raised retry priced 30,000 micros above its admission bound
findings.claim_under_review: packages/ai/src/routing.ts:192-193: "Every `maxCostMicros` here is an ADMISSION bound and nothing else: the largest single request the stage may send"
findings.mechanism: run.ts:273-280 applies `limits.maxCostMicros` only when `attempt === 1`; every later request — including the one raised retry, which is the LARGEST request the stage ever sends — is weighed against the budget alone. Whether a raised retry can then exceed the admission bound is pure arithmetic on the configured pair: the retry's own estimate is at most `budget − rateOut x B` (the cut-off attempt already spent `rateOut x B` at minimum). For nine of the ten stages that number is under the cap, so the sentence happens to hold: extraction/grading 216,816 − 48,000 = 168,816 <= 216,816; verification 76,000 <= 100,000; coaching 282,520 <= 300,000; daily_set 333,240 <= 350,000; thursday_bundle 633,600 <= 700,000; semantic_check 31,200 <= 40,000; adult_summary 18,200 <= 20,000; escalation never retries. followup is the exception: 240,000 − (50 x 1,200) = 180,000 against an admission bound of 150,000. A worked instance: followup admitted at E = 9,000 (estimate 150,000), truncated with 2,000 reported input tokens (spent 80,000), then `raisedOutputBudget` returns 1,400 and sends a single request estimated at 10 x 9,000 + 50 x 1,400 = 160,000 — 10,000 micros above the bound the comment calls "the largest single request the stage may send". The new test that pins this half (`refuses a %s request over its ADMISSION cap even though the stage budget would fit it`, run-truncation.test.ts:297-347) exercises coaching, daily_set and thursday_bundle and only attempt 1, so it cannot see it; run.ts's own JSDoc (run.ts:198-199) is the accurate wording — "`limits.maxCostMicros` alone decides whether the FIRST request is sent".
findings.impact: No production request reaches it today, because followup has no prompt in prompts.ts and no runStage caller — so this is a false sentence about an invariant, plus a trap: the day followup's prompt is written and wired, the stage sends one request 20% above the owner's recorded per-request bound with nothing red, and the comment says that cannot happen.
findings.ruled_out: (a) I checked whether the loop re-applies the cap on later attempts: it does not — the ternary at run.ts:274 keys on `attempt === 1` and on nothing else, and `raisedOutputBudget`'s `admits` (run.ts:153-160) uses the budget too, so both the search and the loop agree on the larger number. (b) I checked whether followup is reachable: `Object.keys(PROMPTS)` is extraction, grading, verification, coaching, adult_summary, daily_set, thursday_bundle (prompts.ts:39-141); grep for runStage across the repo finds only scan-process.ts:1257 and learning-jobs.ts:714, neither of which can pass stage `followup`. (c) I checked the non-truncation retries: they reuse the same `maxOutputTokens`, so their estimate equals attempt 1's and is bounded by the cap by construction — the exposure is the raised retry only. (d) `defineStageCostBudgets` cannot catch it: it compares budget vs cap and budget vs ceiling, never `budget − rateOut x B` vs cap.
findings.reproduction: packages/ai/src/run-truncation.test.ts: for every stage with `maxAttempts >= 2`, assert `PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS[stage] - rateOut(STAGE_MODELS[stage]) * PROPOSED_STAGE_LIMITS[stage].maxOutputTokens <= PROPOSED_STAGE_LIMITS[stage].maxCostMicros` — the stated property "no single request any attempt sends exceeds the admission bound". Red for followup today (180,000 > 150,000), green for the other eight.
findings.suggested_fix: Make the sentence match the code: routing.ts:192-193 should say the cap bounds the FIRST request (the pre-flight admission gate), and that the one raised retry is bounded by the stage budget and can price above the cap where `budget − rateOut x maxOutputTokens` exceeds it — naming followup as the one stage configured that way. If the lead prefers the stronger property, add the invariant above to `defineStageCostBudgets` so the worker refuses to start on such a pair, and set followup's two numbers accordingly. Do not narrow the run-truncation case set.

findings.title: `fullRaiseCeiling` and the startup budget check price against a hardcoded rate table, while run.ts spends at the caller's `rates`, so the guard cannot see the one change that most plausibly reopens BUG-309
findings.claim_under_review: packages/ai/src/routing.ts:222-225: "so a new stage, a raised `maxOutputTokens` or a lowered number fails the worker at startup instead of promising a retry it cannot pay for" and routing.ts:132-133: "It is the exact sum run.ts weighs against the stage BUDGET on that retry"
findings.mechanism: `fullRaiseCeiling` prices both terms against `DEFAULT_RATE_TABLE_2026_09_18` literally (routing.ts:152, 158), and `defineStageCostBudgets` runs once at module import (routing.ts:250). run.ts prices the same two terms against `options.rates`, which every caller supplies: scan-process.ts:1262 passes `this.rates` (`options.rates ?? DEFAULT_RATE_TABLE_2026_09_18`, scan-process.ts:763) and learning-jobs.ts:719 passes `options.rates ?? DEFAULT_RATE_TABLE_2026_09_18`. Rates are explicitly versioned and expected to change (packages/domain/src/quotas/rates.ts:16 "Rate table version; stored with every metered operation"; spec P12 "Keep billing rates in a versioned server table"), and `AttemptRecord.rateTableVersion` exists precisely so a second version can be introduced. On the day a `DEFAULT_RATE_TABLE_<newer>` is added and wired, the startup check still validates the budgets against the September table and passes, while `raisedOutputBudget` prices the retry at the new rates and returns a shrunken budget or null — the BUG-260/BUG-309 failure, silently, with the guard that exists to prevent it green. The enumerated list of what fails at startup (new stage, raised maxOutputTokens, lowered number) omits the rate table, and it is the only input of the three that is not in this file.
findings.impact: Not reachable today — no second rate table exists and no production caller passes one — so nothing a family or the owner meets. It is a hole in the guard the round built, in the exact dimension the guard's own docstring enumerates, and the failure it would let through is the one that already cost two rounds.
findings.ruled_out: (a) I checked that no production path supplies a non-default table: grep for `ModelRateTable`/`RateTable` shows only the default constant, the domain functions and the two optional `rates?` job options, which only tests set. (b) I checked that a rate change is otherwise caught: it is not — `STAGE_MODELS` changes ARE caught (fullRaiseCeiling reads it at routing.ts:150), but a rate row change is invisible to it, and no test asserts the ceiling against the table runStage is handed. (c) I checked that the hold would still bound the spend: it would — runStage bounds cumulative metered cost by the budget whatever the rates, so this degrades retry reachability, not the spend ceiling. That is why it is low and not medium. (d) I verified all ten ceilings against the current table by hand, so the numbers are right FOR this table: 155,972 / 153,264 / 76,796 / 407,520 / 240,000 / 483,240 / 933,600 / 40,800 / 660,000 / 5,861.
findings.reproduction: Mutation rather than a red case today: add a second table (astra 15/75 micros per token) and pass it as `options.rates` to `personalizeItems`; the daily_set raise shrinks and, at its floor input, `raisedOutputBudget` stops returning the full multiple, while `defineStageCostBudgets` still imports clean. A durable case would give `fullRaiseCeiling` a rates parameter and assert every budget against the table the callers actually pass.
findings.suggested_fix: Give `fullRaiseCeiling(stage, maxOutputTokens, rates)` the rate table as a parameter with the September table as the default, and add the rate table to what routing.ts:222-225 says fails at startup — or, if the signature must stay, state plainly in both docstrings that the ceiling is priced against DEFAULT_RATE_TABLE_2026_09_18 and that a new table version must re-derive every budget by hand, with an owner action recorded for it. Either way add one case asserting the budgets against the table the production callers pass.

findings.title: The one copy of the truncation-multiple docstring that moved into routing.ts still says the raise is bounded by "the stage's cost cap", which is the number this same file spent 200 lines separating from the one the raise is actually weighed against
findings.claim_under_review: packages/ai/src/routing.ts:91-94: "once, at up to this multiple of the configured `maxOutputTokens`, and never past what the stage's cost cap still admits — the owner's ceiling is never exceeded to fit a longer answer. It lives here, next to the caps it is spent against"
findings.mechanism: HUNT6-D-1 moved `OUTPUT_TRUNCATED_BUDGET_MULTIPLE` from run.ts to routing.ts. The copy left behind in run.ts was rewritten (run.ts:63-67 now just points at routing.ts) and every other "cost cap" in run.ts was changed to "cost BUDGET" in the same diff (run.ts:56-57, 70, 255, 356). The sentence that travelled to routing.ts:91-94 was not: it still says the raise never goes "past what the stage's cost cap still admits", and adds "next to the caps it is spent against". In this file, after the split, "cap" means `PROPOSED_STAGE_LIMITS[stage].maxCostMicros` (routing.ts:192-193 defines it that way in terms) — and the raise is weighed against `PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS[stage]` instead (run.ts:153-160, 360-370), which for five stages is a strictly larger number the round raised specifically to fit a longer answer. So the sentence asserts the opposite of what the round did, in the docstring of the constant the round moved here, three lines above the cap/budget distinction.
findings.impact: Prose only, and no user meets it. Its cost is the next reader's: it is the first docstring in the file that mentions the raise, it names the wrong one of two deliberately-similar numbers, and it is the shape ("the owner's ceiling is never exceeded to fit a longer answer") that a later change would reasonably be checked against.
findings.ruled_out: (a) Not a second true reading: 'cap' in routing.ts is bound to the admission bound by routing.ts:192-193 and by the budget table's own "WHY THIS IS A SECOND NUMBER" paragraph, so there is no sense in which the raise is bounded by the cap for coaching (300,000) whose raise draws on 407,520. (b) Not already covered by another finding: HUNT6-D-5's fix was the run-truncation.test.ts docstring figure, and HUNT6-D-4's was the EXTRACTION_GRADING_COST_MICROS paragraph at routing.ts:67-78; this is the third, untouched copy. (c) I checked run.ts's re-export does not carry a second stale copy — run.ts:63-67 is only the pointer.
findings.reproduction: No runtime assertion is possible for a comment; the fact the sentence denies is the existing case packages/ai/src/run-truncation.test.ts > 'refuses a %s request over its ADMISSION cap even though the stage budget would fit it', which shows coaching's raise being paid for out of 407,520 while its cap stays at 300,000.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite routing.ts:91-94 to say the raise is bounded by the stage's cost BUDGET (`PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS`), that the budget is sized for exactly this raise, and that the per-request admission cap is never raised to fit a longer answer — the same wording run.ts:70-72 already uses.

findings.title: The new whole-file prose guard scans the dispatcher line by line, so the formatter-wrapped sentence its own comment says must stay visible to the regex is exactly what escapes the negative half
findings.claim_under_review: apps/api/tests/jobs-r2.review.test.ts:427-434: "So this searches the WHOLE FILE, case-insensitively, and reports the offending LINES: no window for the next copy to hide between" (and, in the same case, "Unwrapped, because a sentence a formatter split over two comment lines must still be readable to a regex — otherwise this guard passes on a claim it cannot see (the L-054 shape again)")
findings.mechanism: The negative half builds its offender list per line: `source.split('\n').map((line, index) => …).filter((line) => promises.test(line))` with `promises = /reserved slice|enough for the sweep|always gets a slice|leaves to the steps/i`, then `expect(offenders).toEqual([])`. Every pattern is a multi-word phrase, and the file's comments are wrapped at the repo's print width — the very copy this case was written to catch, "keeping the trailing steps their reserved slice of it" (dispatcher.ts, pre-diff), sits one line from `const remaining` and is exactly the length that wraps. A re-added promise split as "… their reserved" / "// slice of it" matches no single line and the guard stays green. The positive half of the same case defends against precisely this, unwrapping before matching (`.replace(/\s*\/\/\s*/g, ' ').replace(/\s+/g, ' ')` at jobs-r2.review.test.ts:440-443) and says in its comment why. The negative half — the half that is the whole point of the case, and the half HUNT6-D-2 was filed about — does not.
findings.impact: A weak test, not a wrong outcome: no promise is present today (I unwrapped the whole file and searched; zero matches), so the case is not currently vacuous. But it is the only guard standing between the next rewrite and the fourth copy of a claim that has now been re-added three times, and it is blind in exactly the dimension its own comment names.
findings.ruled_out: (a) I verified the guard is not vacuous today: `tr '\n' ' '` over dispatcher.ts with comment markers collapsed, searched for all four phrases plus `reserved.{0,12}slice` — no match, so the file is genuinely clean and the finding is about the guard's reach, not a live offender. (b) I checked the windowed positive assertions cannot compensate: they are scoped to the constants block and to 600 characters before `const remaining`, so a promise anywhere else in the 1,400-line file is the negative half's job alone. (c) I checked the offender strings are not matched against something that would save it: the map prefixes a line number, which no pattern can match, so trimming/prefixing does not widen the match. (d) Not a duplicate of HUNT6-D-2: that finding was about the missing copies; this is about the guard written to replace it.
findings.reproduction: Mutation over the current tree: insert into dispatcher.ts's TICK_TRAILING_RESERVE_MS docstring a wrapped sentence such as "… so the trailing steps keep their reserved" / " * slice of the invocation." — apps/api/tests/jobs-r2.review.test.ts > 'nowhere in the dispatcher promises the trailing steps a reserved slice' stays GREEN, while the same sentence on one line turns it red.
findings.suggested_fix: Unwrap before the negative scan too: normalise the source once (strip `//` and ` * ` comment markers, collapse whitespace) and search that single string, reporting the surrounding context instead of a line number so the failure is still readable — the same normalisation the case already applies to `claimFilter`.

findings.title: Three spend-ceiling cases still size the owner's budget from the ADMISSION caps after production moved its holds to the stage budgets; they are green only because those three stages' two numbers are equal, and routing.ts invites parting them in one line
findings.claim_under_review: apps/api/tests/scan-process.test.ts:1079-1080: "Room for exactly one stage: the owner's cap is recorded spend plus the extraction's upper-bound estimate, so extraction is admitted and grading + verification would cross the cap" (`cap = recorded + PROPOSED_STAGE_LIMITS.extraction.maxCostMicros`)
findings.mechanism: After HUNT6-D-CAP/F-HOLD, the number that has to fit under the owner's monthly ceiling for a scan group to be admitted is the sum of `PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS` (apps/api/src/jobs/scan-process.ts:1232), not the sum of `PROPOSED_STAGE_LIMITS[*].maxCostMicros`. The round-6 diff updated the two learning cases to the budget table (apps/api/tests/learning-jobs.test.ts:656-665, 768-775) and left the three scan cases on the caps: scan-process.test.ts:1072-1080 ("the spend ceiling pauses a scan without spending an attempt"), :2020-2058 (LJA-F4, summing extraction + grading + verification caps) and :2111-2113 (LJA-F5). They pass because extraction, grading and verification are the three stages whose admission cap and budget are the same number (216,816 / 216,816 / 100,000). routing.ts:84-86 records parting them as a supported one-line owner change — "give these two stages `maxCostMicros: 150_000` and leave the budget at 216,816" — and that configuration is legal (budget >= cap and >= the 155,972 ceiling, so `defineStageCostBudgets` and runStage's RangeError both accept it). The moment it is made, these cases build a ceiling of 150,000 while the hold asks for 216,816, so extraction is refused at `acquireSpendHold` and the cases fail while asserting the opposite of what they mean.
findings.impact: No user outcome: the three cases are green and their assertions are currently correct. The cost is a fixer's next round — the owner change routing.ts advertises turns three unrelated scan cases red for a reason none of them names, and the premise the cases state in prose ("room for exactly one stage") is no longer the number they compute.
findings.ruled_out: (a) I verified the numbers really coincide today, so this is latent and not a live failure: extraction and grading budgets are `EXTRACTION_GRADING_COST_MICROS` (routing.ts:308-309) and verification's is 100,000 (routing.ts:310), equal to their caps; the LJA-F4 sum 533,632 equals the two holds 216,816 + 316,816. (b) I checked the production side was updated: `spending()` sums the budget table (scan-process.ts:1232) and `personalizeItems` reserves it (learning-jobs.ts:678) — the gap is only in these test call sites. (c) I checked apps/api/tests/spend-ceiling.test.ts: it uses bare literals against `acquireSpendHold` directly and does not reference either table, so it is not affected. (d) The mutation is legal, not a straw man: cap 150,000 with budget 216,816 passes `defineStageCostBudgets` (216,816 >= 150,000 and >= 155,972) and passes runStage's cap-above-budget check.
findings.reproduction: Mutation over the current tree: in packages/ai/src/routing.ts give extraction and grading `maxCostMicros: 150_000` while leaving PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS at 216,816 — the change routing.ts:84-86 describes. apps/api/tests/scan-process.test.ts > 'the spend ceiling pauses a scan without spending an attempt…' goes red on `expect(client.requests.map(r => r.outputName)).toEqual(['homework_extraction'])` because the hold (216,816) no longer fits the ceiling the case built (150,000).
findings.suggested_fix: Change the three scan spend-ceiling cases to build the owner's budget from `PROPOSED_STAGE_COST_BUDGET_MICROS` — extraction alone at :1080 and :2113, and extraction + grading + verification at :2056-2058 — and update their comments to say the reservation is the stage BUDGET, matching the wording the round already gave the two learning cases. While there, the stale figure in the sibling case at :2078 ("grading (150,000 micros) fits") should name grading's current 216,816.
