findings.title: The refund walk spills on the primary period's bucket SIZE, not what the bucket has LEFT, so a chargeback after any earlier refund never reaches the ':proration' row and clawed-back money reads as kept revenue
findings.claim_under_review: "C-PRORATION-REVERSAL: what this period's own bucket cannot absorb, still in the caller's unit — its charge plus, when the amount is tax-inclusive, the tax stored on that charge, which together are the most of a provider figure this period can account for." (billing-sync.ts:1029-1032) and "whatever is LEFT of the provider's amount above that period's bucket ... then reaches the ':proration' period" (billing-sync.ts:1131-1135)
findings.mechanism: `applySettlementToPeriod` computes `leftoverCents = max(0, refundedCents - current.charged_amount_cents - tax)` (apps/api/src/services/billing-sync.ts:1033-1041). The row's own `refunded_cents` is not in the computation and is not even selected: the FOR UPDATE select at billing-sync.ts:993-995 reads only `id, charged_amount_cents, tax_amount_cents, settlement`. So the leftover is measured against the period's total capacity rather than its remaining capacity. For a REFUND that is harmless, because Stripe's `Charge.amount_refunded` is cumulative and the SQL uses `greatest(refunded_cents, inCharge)` (billing-sync.ts:1091), so the caller's amount already covers everything refunded before it. A CHARGEBACK is the opposite: `charge.dispute.created` states only the newly disputed part (webhooks.ts:380-386) and the SQL ADDS it on top, capped: `least(charged_amount_cents, refunded_cents + coalesce(inCharge, charged_amount_cents))` (billing-sync.ts:1089-1090). When `refunded_cents + inCharge` exceeds the charge, the cap silently swallows the excess AND the leftover is 0, so `applyRefund`'s spill at billing-sync.ts:1178-1179 (`if (leftover !== null && leftover <= 0) return`) never runs and the `<invoice>:proration` row written by `prorationPeriodFor` (billing-sync.ts:479-490) is left settled with refunded_cents 0. The invoice's provider amounts are scaled to charge + pending net + tax, while the primary period's cap is its own charge alone, so on every deferred-proration invoice the sum routinely exceeds the cap.
findings.impact: On an invoice that carried a deferred mid-cycle proration, a partial refund followed by a dispute of the un-refunded remainder claws back every cent the family paid, while the owner's revenue page records only the subscription part: gross 4999, refunds 3999, net 1000 for money that is entirely gone. That is the exact hole the same docstring says it closed ("a FULLY refunded renewal that had carried a deferred proration left that money in gross with nothing reversing it: clawed-back money reading as kept revenue") — still open through the one ordering the change did not name. It is also silently unreconcilable: the Stripe dashboard shows 4999 reversed and PencilLift shows 3999, with no row the owner can point at.
findings.ruled_out: 1) I checked the refund path separately and it is sound: `Charge.amount_refunded` is cumulative and the partial/full branches use `greatest(...)`, so two successive partial refunds spill correctly (2000 then 4500 → proration row 501 then 801). The defect is confined to the ADD-on-top chargeback branch. 2) I checked that the primary really is capped and the excess really is lost, not deferred: billing-sync.ts:1089-1090 is `least(charged_amount_cents, refunded_cents + …)` with no second write, and `applyRefund` (billing-sync.ts:1163-1191) makes exactly one secondary call whose amount is `primary.leftoverCents`. 3) I checked it is not rescued by a later event: the reversal branch (billing-sync.ts:1080-1082) only subtracts, and `pending_refunds` is never written for the derived id (park=false at billing-sync.ts:1187, guarded at billing-sync.ts:1000-1002). 4) I checked the repro does not depend on the unverified Stripe assumption at billing-hardening.review.test.ts:392 ("Stripe disputes at most the un-refunded remainder"): webhooks.ts:377-379 states Stripe allows partial disputes, and any dispute amount with refunded_cents + inCharge > charged reproduces it; if Stripe instead disputes the full charge total the leftover is positive and this particular case does not fire, which is why the repro uses the remainder the codebase itself assumes. 5) I checked the $1 school donation is not the mechanism here: `planAccruals` (packages/domain/src/donations/accruals.ts:92-130) rejects the proration row via `evaluateDonationEligibility`'s subscription_period rule (packages/domain/src/donations/eligibility.ts:195), so this is purely the money figure. 6) I checked every other reader of `billing_periods` handles the new kind (revenue query, 0690/0730/0740 school functions, p17-jobs, promotions-data, admin-ops) — none of them compensates, because the money was recorded and then not reversed.
findings.reproduction: apps/api/tests/billing-r2.review.test.ts, describe 'C-PRORATION-REVERSAL: a provider refund reaches BOTH periods of one invoice'. Add a case beside 'a partial refund that fits inside the primary period leaves the proration row alone', with tax 0 for exact integers: invoice.paid `in_X` {billing_reason subscription_cycle, subtotal 4999, tax 0, amount_paid 4999, lines [{proration true, amount 1000}, {price price_family_1, amount 3999}]} → rows `in_X` 3999 and `in_X:proration` 1000, gross +4999. Then charge.refunded {amount 4999, amount_refunded 1000, refunded false} → primary refunded_cents 1000. Then charge.dispute.created {amount 3999}. Assert `rows[1]` (the ':proration' row) `{ settlement: 'chargeback', refunded_cents: 1000 }` and `after.refunds - before.refunds === 4999`: today it is red at `{ settlement: 'settled', refunded_cents: 0 }` and 3999.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `refunded_cents` to the FOR UPDATE select at billing-sync.ts:993-995 and give each period only what it can still absorb, passing the rest on: for an ADD-on-top event (`chargeback`) the amount this period accounts for is `min(inCharge, charged_amount_cents - refunded_cents)` plus, for a tax-inclusive figure, its tax share, and the leftover handed to the ':proration' row is the caller's amount less that. Leave the cumulative branches (`refund`, `partial_refund`) measuring against the whole bucket, since their figures are cumulative — and say so in the comment, because one expression is currently serving both an incremental and a cumulative figure. Then correct the two prose claims (billing-sync.ts:1029-1032 and the bullet list at billing-sync.ts:1136-1143) to say which figures are cumulative and which are incremental. Do not weaken the existing cap: every per-row figure must still be capped at that row's charge.

findings.title: On a deferred-proration invoice a won dispute erases a genuine partial refund and reinstates the school's $1, and the parent is then told the store has reported no refund at all — HUNT6-C-2's own defect, reopened by HUNT6-C-1's second period
findings.claim_under_review: "HUNT6-C-2: that round trip holds only because the dispute amount is restated in the same unit as the refund beside it (amountIsTaxInclusive above)." (billing-sync.ts:1045-1049) and "Every figure then holds one unit, so a chargeback that ADDS and a won dispute that SUBTRACTS round-trip: they are the same number." (billing-sync.ts:967-970)
findings.mechanism: The chargeback ADDS and caps — `least(charged_amount_cents, refunded_cents + coalesce(inCharge, charged_amount_cents))` (billing-sync.ts:1089-1090) — while the won dispute SUBTRACTS the whole converted amount — `greatest(0, refunded_cents - coalesce(inCharge, charged_amount_cents))` (billing-sync.ts:1080-1082, and the same expression decides the settlement at billing-sync.ts:1071-1074). The round trip is exact only while `refunded_cents + inCharge <= charged_amount_cents`; the unit conversion (the round-6 fix) guarantees that only when the provider's charge total equals `charged + tax`, i.e. on an invoice with no other lines. HUNT6-C-1's `prorationPeriodFor` (billing-sync.ts:479-490) created exactly the invoice shape where it does not: the provider total is `charged + pending net + tax` while the primary's cap is `charged`, so a dispute of the un-refunded remainder converts to more than the primary can hold, the cap clips it, and the win subtracts the unclipped figure. Tax 0 for clarity: charge 3999 with a 1000 ':proration' sibling, refund 1000 → refunded 1000; dispute 3999 → least(3999, 1000+3999) = 3999 (1000 clipped); win 3999 → greatest(0, 3999-3999) = 0 and settlement back to 'settled'. The family's real $10 refund is gone from the record. Because `refunded_cents` lands at exactly 0 with settlement 'settled', `planAdjustment`'s `settledInFull` (packages/domain/src/donations/adjustments.ts:120-124) is true and the $1 school donation reversed at the refund is REINSTATED. This also falsifies the round-6 hunt's own not-a-false-positive note for HUNT6-C-2 ("planAdjustment reinstates only when refundedCents === 0, so the $1 school donation is NOT wrongly reinstated here"). Before this diff the same three events produced a correct aggregate — gross 3999, refunds 0, net 3999, which is what PencilLift really kept — because the proration money was in no month's gross; adding it to gross without fixing the round trip is what made the figure wrong.
findings.impact: A parent who received a partial refund and then lost a chargeback reads, on their own support case, "The store has not reported a refund on this charge yet" (apps/web/src/pages/app/SupportPage.tsx:445-447; the mobile wording is apps/mobile/src/support/view-model.ts:163-164) although the store refunded them — a false statement about their account and their money, on the one surface built to tell them what the provider reported. The admin case detail shows the same 0. The owner's revenue page overstates net by the full proration amount (1000 cents in the example, not the 178 cents HUNT6-C-2 was closed over), and a school is paid a $1 donation for a month in which the family was partly refunded, which is the one thing the P17 reversal exists to prevent.
findings.ruled_out: 1) I checked whether this is pre-existing rather than a round-6 regression, and it is a regression in its observable effect: the primary row's arithmetic is unchanged, but before this diff the proration money was in no month's gross, so gross 3999 / refunds 0 was the correct aggregate; now gross is 4999 and refunds 0, so the same clipping produces a wrong number. 2) I checked the new taxed test that claims to pin the round trip — apps/api/tests/billing-hardening.review.test.ts 'taxed: refund half the charge, dispute the other half, win it' — and its fixture has NO proration line (subtotal 4998, tax 412, amount_paid 5410), so charge total = charged + tax exactly and the two halves convert to 2499 + 2499 = 4998, the cap to the cent. Its own comment says the amounts were chosen so rounding cannot bite; the cap therefore never bites either, and no test anywhere combines a dispute with a deferred-proration invoice (the only new dispute case, billing-r2.review.test.ts 'a dispute of the whole charge, and the win that follows it, round-trip across both rows', disputes the WHOLE 5411 with no prior refund, which spills correctly). 3) I checked that HUNT7-C-1's fix does not close this: with the spill corrected the chargeback would add 2999 to the primary and 1000 to the proration row, but the win still subtracts the full converted 3999 from the primary's 3999 → 0, so the genuine refund is still erased. They are separate defects. 4) I checked it holds under both readings of Stripe's dispute amount: if Stripe disputes the full charge total 4999 instead of the remainder, the primary is still clipped (least(3999, 1000+3999)) and the win still subtracts 3999 → 0. 5) I checked `planAdjustment` cannot double-reverse instead: with 'reversal' already written, a 'chargeback' returns null (adjustments.ts:112-116), so the reinstatement is the only adjustment the win writes. 6) I confirmed the row the parent sees is the primary one they would pick (support.ts:118-123 joins on the case's channel + provider_period_id).
findings.reproduction: apps/api/tests/billing-r2.review.test.ts, describe 'C-PRORATION-REVERSAL…': continue the HUNT7-C-1 sequence (invoice `in_X` 3999 + `in_X:proration` 1000, tax 0; charge.refunded amount_refunded 1000; charge.dispute.created amount 3999) with charge.dispute.closed status 'won' amount 3999, and assert `rows[0]` is `{ settlement: 'partially_refunded', refunded_cents: 1000 }` and `after.refunds - before.refunds === 1000`. Today it is red at `{ settlement: 'settled', refunded_cents: 0 }` and 0. Run `runDonationAccrual` for the month before the refund and assert no `donation_adjustments` row of kind 'reinstatement' exists; today one is written.
findings.suggested_fix: A won dispute must give back what the dispute actually added, and that figure is not recoverable from a single `refunded_cents` column once the cap has clipped it: ask the lead for a migration number and record the dispute's own contribution (a `chargeback_cents integer not null default 0` beside `refunded_cents`, or separate refund/chargeback columns), so `chargeback` adds `min(inCharge, charged - refunded)` and stores what it added, and `chargeback_reversed` subtracts exactly that, leaving any earlier genuine refund untouched. Until that column exists the round trip is only correct while `refunded_cents + inCharge <= charged_amount_cents`, so at minimum state that precondition in the comment at billing-sync.ts:1045-1049 instead of claiming the unit alone makes the two the same number, and pair it with HUNT7-C-1's spill so the excess is recorded somewhere rather than dropped. Note that the same asymmetry also costs one cent on a single-period taxed charge when the two halves each round half up (already recorded as the residual of BUG-306); the column fixes both. Do not weaken the cap or the existing BILL-R1-1 assertions.

findings.title: The parent's refund-request picker now lists the derived ':proration' row as a second, unlabelled charge for the same dates, ordered against the real charge by a random uuid
findings.claim_under_review: "GET /v1/support/billing-periods: the family's periods, newest first (empty without a purchase)." (packages/contracts/src/support.ts:102) and "A family's own billing period as the parent picks it for a refund request" (packages/contracts/src/support.ts:87)
findings.mechanism: `prorationPeriodFor` (apps/api/src/services/billing-sync.ts:479-490) writes the second row with `...period` spread, so it inherits the subscription period's `period_start`, `period_end`, `paid_slots` and `settled_at`, differing only in `provider_period_id`, `kind` and `charged_amount_cents`. GET /v1/support/billing-periods (apps/api/src/routes/support.ts:183-190) selects every row for the family with no kind filter and `order by period_start desc, id desc`; because both rows of one invoice share `period_start`, the tie is broken by `id`, which is `gen_random_uuid()` (supabase/migrations/0200_billing.sql:167), so the order between them is random per family. `supportBillingPeriodSchema` is a `strictObject` with no `kind` (packages/contracts/src/support.ts:87-99), so neither client can label the row: the web picker renders `Stripe · Sep 19 – Oct 19 · $10.00` beside `Stripe · Sep 19 – Oct 19 · $39.99` (apps/web/src/pages/app/SupportPage.tsx:125-128) and the mobile label renders `Stripe · Sep 19 to Oct 19 · $10.00 for 1 child` (apps/mobile/src/support/view-model.ts:147-149) — a sentence that is false about the row, since that $10 is a mid-cycle item from the PREVIOUS period and not a period charge for those dates. The admin surface was given the label (apps/web/src/pages/admin/SupportAdminPage.tsx:1200 renders `p.kind`) and the admin contract carries the enum (packages/contracts/src/admin-ops.ts:327); the parent surface was not. This is L-037: one new row, two surfaces, one of them swept.
findings.impact: A parent opening a refund request for their $39.99 renewal sees two entries for the same dates and, half the time, the $10 one on top of the list they are told is newest-first. If they pick it, the case is linked to the proration period, the case detail then says "Charge in question: Stripe · Sep 19 – Oct 19 · $10.00", and staff assess a refund of the wrong amount against the wrong row — while the parent's own request was about $39.99. Every refund figure and settlement the parent reads on that case is then the proration row's, not their subscription charge's.
findings.ruled_out: 1) I checked that the row is genuinely parent-visible and not blocked by RLS: billing_periods has a member read policy (supabase/migrations/0200_billing.sql:322) and the query runs `asParent`, so the row is returned; the 0810 refund-request check (supabase/migrations/0810_support_cases.sql:150-156) also accepts it, since it only requires the period to belong to the family. 2) I checked whether a kind filter is the right fix and it is not sufficient on its own: an immediately invoiced mid-cycle change is a real separate Stripe charge already recorded with kind 'proration' (mapStripeInvoiceToPeriod, billing-sync.ts:423-429, pinned by billing-r2.review.test.ts 'a standalone proration invoice is counted once in gross'), so filtering kind = 'subscription_period' would hide a charge a parent legitimately wants refunded. 3) I checked the admin path is unaffected (admin-ops.ts:322-325 selects and returns `kind`, the contract permits 'proration', the page prints it). 4) I checked no existing test would catch this: apps/api/tests/support.test.ts:90-106 seeds only subscription periods and asserts the two ids in order, and apps/web/src/pages/app/SupportPage.test.tsx supplies a single period. 5) I confirmed the ordering tie is real rather than stable-by-insert: Postgres gives no order guarantee, `id desc` is a random uuid, and the two rows are inserted in the same transaction (webhooks.ts:328-337).
findings.reproduction: apps/api/tests/support.test.ts, describe 'intake': after posting the deferred-proration invoice.paid used in billing-r2.review.test.ts (`in_X` 3999 plus `in_X:proration` 1000), assert `body.periods.map((p) => p.providerPeriodId)` contains only the subscription id, or — if the lead chooses labelling over filtering — assert `body.periods[0].kind === 'subscription_period'` and that the proration entry carries a kind the client can render. Both are red today: the response has two indistinguishable entries and `kind` is not in the strictObject at all.
findings.suggested_fix: Decide what the parent picker is a list of, and make the response say it. Preferred: add `kind` to `supportBillingPeriodSchema` (it is already in the admin contract) and render a distinct label for a proration entry in both clients, so a parent can see which row is their subscription charge; keep the derived ':proration' row out of the pick list itself (match on the row's id, not its kind, so a standalone proration invoice stays pickable) or order the list by `period_start desc, charged_amount_cents desc, id desc` so the real charge is never below its sibling. Also fix the mobile label so it does not describe a proration amount as "$10.00 for 1 child" over the subscription period's dates.

findings.title: The ':proration' row is given taxCents 0 on the stated ground that no restatement is needed there, so the tax-inclusive leftover is written straight against a pre-tax charge — and the test comment beside the row still says no refund reaches it
findings.claim_under_review: "It carries no tax: US sales tax is never revenue, and the tax figure exists only so a provider refund amount can be restated in the charge's unit (`preTaxRefundCents`), and this row's charge is already in that unit." (billing-sync.ts:471-473); and "a refund of this invoice is recorded against the subscription period, which is the row that holds the provider's figure" (apps/api/tests/billing-r2.review.test.ts:1459-1460); and the owner-facing "every provider figure restated in that same pre-tax unit and capped at the charge" (ops-metrics.ts:171)
findings.mechanism: `prorationPeriodFor` sets `taxCents: 0` (billing-sync.ts:486) and justifies it by the row's CHARGE already being pre-tax — but the figure that now reaches the row is the leftover, which billing-sync.ts:1029-1030 says explicitly is "still in the caller's unit", i.e. tax-inclusive. With `taxCents` 0, `preTaxRefundCents` short-circuits at billing-sync.ts:921-923 and returns it unchanged, so the one row whose whole purpose is to hold pre-tax collected money records refunds in the provider's unit. On the fixture the new tests use (subtotal 4999, tax 412, amount_paid 5411 → primary 3999/tax 329, proration 1000/tax 0, the proration's own tax share 83), a partial refund of 4400 gives leftover 4400-3999-329 = 72 written against the 1000 charge, where the true pre-tax spill is round(4400x4999/5411) - 3999 = 66: 6 cents too much. I checked the direction algebraically — the secondary is reached only when the amount exceeds 4328, and leftover - true spill = amount x tax_total/(charge_total+tax_total) - tax_primary, which is >= 0 for every amount above 4321 — so it always OVER-records the refund, i.e. net revenue understated, the safe direction, and it is bounded by the row's own cap (so a full refund is exact). Separately, the same diff falsified its own test comment: billing-r2.review.test.ts:1459-1460 tells the next reader that a refund of this invoice is recorded against the subscription period, while billing-sync.ts:1178-1190 and the C-PRORATION-REVERSAL cases at billing-r2.review.test.ts assert refunded_cents 1000 on this very row.
findings.impact: The owner's refunds column is a few cents high on any partial refund large enough to spill onto a deferred-proration row, so a Stripe reconciliation is off by the proration item's tax share; the parent's case detail shows the same few cents. The bigger cost is the prose: the justification given for taxCents 0 is about the wrong side of the conversion, and a reader who trusts the test comment beside the row will conclude no refund reaches it — which is what the last two rounds' worst defects were made of.
findings.ruled_out: 1) I checked the direction cannot be the unsafe one: proved above that the leftover is never below the true pre-tax spill whenever the secondary is reached, so clawed-back money can never read as kept revenue through this path. 2) I checked the figure cannot make net go negative: every row's refunded_cents is capped at its own charged_amount_cents (billing-sync.ts:1084-1091), so summed refunds can never exceed summed gross in loadRevenueMonths (ops-metrics.ts:203-206). 3) I checked a full refund is exact: leftover = pending net + (whole tax - apportioned share) >= pending net, and the cap takes it back to the charge (verified against billing-r2.review.test.ts 'a fully refunded renewal reverses its deferred proration too'). 4) I checked that storing the proration row's real tax share instead of 0 would not double-count tax as revenue: `tax_amount_cents` is read only inside applyRefund (billing-sync.ts:993) and is excluded from every other select, so it is not a revenue figure. 5) I checked no test pins the current 6-cent behaviour, so correcting it breaks nothing: the only spill cases assert a full refund (leftover capped) or no spill at all.
findings.reproduction: apps/api/tests/billing-r2.review.test.ts, describe 'C-PRORATION-REVERSAL…', using the existing `renewalWithDeferredProration` fixture: post charge.refunded {amount 5411, amount_refunded 4400, refunded false} and assert `rows[1].refunded_cents === 66` (the pre-tax share of the spill). It is red at 72 today. For the prose half, a case asserting that the comment at billing-r2.review.test.ts:1459-1460 no longer says a refund is recorded against the subscription period would be red today, since it does.
findings.suggested_fix: Decide which is TRUE (L-053). Either store the proration row's own tax share (invoice tax minus the subscription line's apportioned share) so `preTaxRefundCents` restates the leftover exactly as it does on the primary and the owner-facing promise of one unit holds on both rows — and rewrite billing-sync.ts:471-473 to justify the figure by the unit of the amount that reaches the row, not by the unit of its charge; or convert the leftover to the pre-tax unit before handing it to the secondary call at billing-sync.ts:1180-1188 and say so. Either way correct the test comment at apps/api/tests/billing-r2.review.test.ts:1459-1460, which describes the pre-C-PRORATION-REVERSAL behaviour as current.

findings.title: BUG-305's residual in the Bug Ledger still records the unfixed behaviour as current: it says a refund reaches only the subscription period and that the sibling row was deliberately not spread onto
findings.claim_under_review: "A refund/dispute names the invoice id, so it still reaches only the subscription period; I did not spread a refund onto the sibling row (see residuals) because that widens applyRefund and webhooks beyond the lead's decision." (docs/Bug_Ledger.md, BUG-305, last column)
findings.mechanism: BUG-305's row records the same fix twice: its own FIX column reports the first fixer's work, and two later Re-fix sections in the same row record C-PRORATION-REVERSAL and C-NEGATIVE-NET from `wf_9091459c-825`. The residual column was not updated with them, so it still states as present-tense fact that a refund reaches only the subscription period. The shipped code does the opposite: `applyRefund` (apps/api/src/services/billing-sync.ts:1163-1191) derives `<invoice>:proration` and applies the leftover to it, and apps/api/tests/billing-r2.review.test.ts asserts refunded_cents 1000 on that row in three cases. CLAUDE.md names docs/Bug_Ledger.md as a record to read on resume and reconcile with Git, so this is the sentence a round-8 finder or fixer will read first about whether the proration row is reachable by a refund — and it will send them to look for a hole that is (partly) closed, while the real holes are the two filed above.
findings.impact: The next round starts from a false statement about the code in the one record it is told to trust, which is how HUNT6-C-4's "recorded as an open item" defect arose in the first place. It also hides the fact that the feature was extended twice after its own fixer declined to extend it, which is exactly the history a reader needs in order to distrust it.
findings.ruled_out: 1) I checked the code really does spread the refund, so the ledger and not the code is wrong: the suffix constant (billing-sync.ts:461), the derived lookup (billing-sync.ts:1184) and the three asserting cases in billing-r2.review.test.ts. 2) I checked the residual is not merely historical framing: the sentence is present tense ("it still reaches only") and the row's status is "closed (residual in Next)", i.e. it is presented as what remains true after the round. 3) I checked no other record corrects it: `grep -rn 'C-PRORATION-REVERSAL' docs/` returns only this row, so there is no separate entry a reader would find instead. 4) I checked the C-NEGATIVE-NET half is recorded (it is, in the Re-fix text), so only the residual is stale — a one-sentence correction, not a re-write.
findings.reproduction: No test covers the ledger. The check is textual: BUG-305's residual asserts a property of apps/api/src/services/billing-sync.ts that billing-r2.review.test.ts 'a fully refunded renewal reverses its deferred proration too, so net is zero' disproves — the assertion `expect(rows[1]).toMatchObject({ provider_period_id: `${invoiceId}:proration`, settlement: 'refunded', refunded_cents: 1000 })` passes today, which is the opposite of what the residual says.
findings.suggested_fix: The lead (the only owner of docs/) replaces BUG-305's residual with what is now true: the refund walk exists, what it does (primary first in its own unit and capped, leftover to the ':proration' row, nothing parked against the derived id), and the residuals that really remain — HUNT7-C-1 (the leftover is measured against the bucket's size, not what is left of it) and HUNT7-C-2 (a won dispute can still erase an earlier refund on such an invoice).

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The ':proration' period is written at most once per invoice, so the money it holds is counted exactly once (prorationPeriodFor's docstring, billing-sync.ts:466-469).
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Replayed invoice.paid under a new event id; looked for a second writer of the derived id; checked the parked-refund replay inside recordBillingPeriod for the derived id; checked whether a later delivery with different lines could change the amount; checked whether an immediately invoiced proration (billing_reason subscription_update) could also be listed as pending on the next renewal; checked the on-conflict clause for a family_id guard.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: `unique (channel, provider_period_id)` (supabase/migrations/0200_billing.sql:187) plus `on conflict … do update` that touches only `settlement` and `settled_at` (billing-sync.ts:742-745), so a retry can neither add a row nor change `charged_amount_cents`. webhooks.ts:328-337 is the only writer and runs once per invoice.paid. Nothing ever parks against the derived id (park=false at billing-sync.ts:1187, guarded at billing-sync.ts:1000-1002), so the replay delete at billing-sync.ts:761-765 finds nothing for it. `kind` 'proration' is already permitted by the column's CHECK (0200_billing.sql:171), so no migration gap.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The two periods one invoice can write never sum above the pre-tax money it collected (collectedPreTaxCents' docstring, billing-sync.ts:262-267).
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Tried a negative customer credit BALANCE; a net proration CREDIT line; an invoice-level coupon; a line-level discount on the proration line only (pendingProrationNetCents sums `l.amount` and never subtracts each line's own discount_amounts, billing-sync.ts:407-417); the credit-line-first vs charge-line-first tie in subscriptionLine (billing-sync.ts:232-240, where equal period.start keeps the first line); a 100%-off invoice with amount_paid 0; a tax-inclusive pricing shape; a missing `tax` field.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Both figures are bounded by the same collection: charge <= collected (billing-sync.ts:274-275) and net <= collected - charge (billing-sync.ts:415-416). The discount gap is rescued by that bound in every shape the product can bill, because when the subscription line is unclipped `collected - charge` equals the proration lines' real net. The credit-first tie gives charge 0 and net = collected, the charge-first tie gives charge = collected and net 0 — the sum is the collection either way. The one silent escape is `cents(invoice.amount_paid)` returning null for a non-safe-integer or absent `amount_paid` (billing-sync.ts:271-272), which turns BOTH bounds off at once; it needs malformed Stripe data behind a valid signature, and the docstring says so.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: A FULL provider refund always reaches both rows, so a fully refunded renewal keeps nothing of its deferred proration in gross (billing-sync.ts:1136-1143).
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Computed the leftover for a full refund with tax apportionment (5411 - 3999 - 329 = 1083 against a 1000 charge); tried a credit balance that clips the charge so the leftover could vanish; tried a dispute with no amount at all; tried the parked-refund ordering where the refund is delivered before its invoice; tried a chargeback_reversed arriving before either row exists.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: When the bound clips the charge to the collection the pending net is 0 and no second row exists, so leftover 0 and no row are consistent; when the charge is unclipped the leftover is pending net + (whole tax - apportioned share) >= pending net > 0. A null amount propagates as null and means "the whole charge" on both rows (billing-sync.ts:1178). The proration row is written BEFORE the primary (webhooks.ts:328-331), so the parked replay inside recordBillingPeriod has somewhere to spill to; and a won dispute with no primary row returns applied:false before the walk (billing-sync.ts:1000-1002).

properties_attacked_and_held.property: Every reader of public.billing_periods handles the new kind (the brief's question 3).
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Enumerated every read in the repository: loadRevenueMonths (ops-metrics.ts:203-216), the two p17-jobs queries (p17-jobs.ts:272-275 and 299-303), promotions-data.ts:44-47, admin-ops.ts:322-325 and its contract enum, support.ts:118-123 and 183-190, webhooks.ts:262-265, the three school-report SQL functions (0690:54-60, 0730:165-173, 0740:70-84), the 0810 refund-request RLS check, the P16 recognized-revenue path, the privacy export, and the store-fee estimate.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Every aggregate that must exclude a proration either filters `kind = 'subscription_period'` in SQL (the three school functions, the donation family-selection query, promotions-data) or hands the row to `evaluateDonationEligibility`, whose subscription_period rule (eligibility.ts:195) rejects it without consuming the month in planAccruals (accruals.ts:114-122) — so the $1 school donation is untouched, which I verified end to end including the sort tie (`inv` < `inv:proration`, accruals.ts:82-86). The revenue query deliberately has no kind filter. admin-ops selects and returns `kind` and the admin page prints it. The Stripe fee estimate cannot be double-charged by a second row because it is a pure rate on (gross - refunds) with no per-transaction component (packages/domain/src/ops/revenue.ts:73-81, DEFAULT_STRIPE_FEE_RATE 0). `withinRefundWindow` has no production caller. The one reader that does not handle it is the parent picker, filed as HUNT7-C-3.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: `amountIsTaxInclusive` is stated at every call site rather than defaulted, so no path records a figure in the wrong unit (webhooks.ts:540-542, billing-sync.ts:905-914).
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Enumerated all eleven callers of applyRefund in the repository. Production: webhooks.ts:363-370 (charge.refunded, true), :386 (dispute created, true), :390-398 (dispute won, true), :543-551 (RevenueCat, false), billing-sync.ts:768-775 (parked replay, `period.channel === 'stripe'`). Tests: billing-hardening.review.test.ts:185, :312, :316, :324, :335 and admin-promotions.test.ts:324, all of which omit the argument and take the `= false` default (billing-sync.ts:1161). Checked whether a store-channel row could ever be parked with a tax-inclusive amount, and whether pending_refunds' `greatest()` merge could mix units.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Every production call site passes the flag explicitly and correctly: only the Stripe charge/dispute paths are tax-inclusive, RevenueCat passes a null amount, and the parked replay's predicate is exact because only the Stripe path ever parks a stripe-channel row with an amount. The six test callers that rely on the default are all store channels or null amounts, where `false` is the right value and no conversion happens; billing-hardening.review.test.ts:335 is channel 'stripe' but with a null amount, so the default is inert. The default itself remains a trap for a future Stripe call site and no test would catch it, but it is not wrong anywhere today, so I did not file it.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: Integer cents throughout, with no division or float that can lose a cent unsafely (the brief's question 5).
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Audited every arithmetic site the diff added or changed: collectedPreTaxCents (billing-sync.ts:270-274), pendingProrationNetCents (407-417), subscriptionTaxCents' floor (378-384), preTaxRefundCents' single Math.round (917-928), the leftover subtraction (1033-1041), and the SQL least/greatest chain (1076-1092). Bounded the products at the approved prices; looked for a rate ever materialised as a float; recomputed the HUNT6-C-4 figures (floor(100x3999/4999) = 79, preTaxRefundCents(2000,true,3999,79) = 1961) and the taxed BILL-R1-1 halves (2705x4998/5410 = 2499 exactly).
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Every figure is an integer sum, Math.min/max, Math.floor or a single Math.round over an integer quotient; the largest product is about 5x10^7, far inside the safe-integer range, and no fractional rate is ever formed. The tax apportionment floors, which can only shrink the stored tax and so only over-record a refund by at most a cent — the safe direction. The leftover is pure integer subtraction. The one place rounding does bite is two independent half-up conversions of the parts of one charge summing to charge+1, which the cap then clips and the reversal over-subtracts; that one-cent case is already recorded as the residual of BUG-306, and its 1000-cent form on a deferred-proration invoice is filed as HUNT7-C-2 rather than duplicated here.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The owner-facing note and definition now promise one unit for every refund figure, within their length caps, and cannot be satisfied by a rewrite that also satisfies the old claims (ops-metrics.ts:161, :171).
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Measured both strings against the contract caps; ran the new tests' regexes against the shipped strings, including the negative ones `not.toMatch(/proration[^.]*never revenue/)`, `not.toMatch(/at its own amount/)` and `not.toMatch(/where the provider states the charge total/)`; checked whether the `--` SQL comment block added to loadRevenueMonths could break the statement or interpolate anything.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: The note is 392 of 400 characters and the definition 562 of 600, both parsed against the contract schemas rather than a copied number. The bounded negative assertion genuinely cannot match the new note, because "never revenue" precedes "proration" and a sentence boundary separates them; the paired positive assertions pin the true copy, so the two cannot both be satisfied by reverting. The new comment block (ops-metrics.ts:212-221) is entirely `--` lines with no `${}` placeholder. The claim "every provider figure restated in that same pre-tax unit" is however false on the ':proration' row, which is filed as HUNT7-C-4.

findings.title: 0920/0930 withdraw only exports that are ALREADY 'ready'; an export that becomes 'ready' after the request re-opens exactly the window the migration exists to close, and the 'queued rows are safe' justification is false
findings.claim_under_review: "A 'queued' row is left alone because the builder already leaves out every child with an open deletion request." (0930:153-154, identical text at 0920:119-120; and 0920:29-30 "A 'queued' export is untouched: the builder leaves out every child with an open deletion request (privacy.ts)")
findings.mechanism: The withdrawal added by 0920 and carried into 0930 is `update public.data_exports set status = 'expired' ... where family_id = p_family and status = 'ready' and (...)` (supabase/migrations/0930_deletion_lock_order.sql:163-168). It is a point-in-time filter on `status = 'ready'`, so a row that is 'queued' at the instant of the request is untouched — and nothing stops that row from becoming 'ready' afterwards. THE PATH: (1) `public.request_deletion` cancels jobs with `status in ('queued','failed_retryable') and (p_child is null or child_id = p_child)` (0930:118-120). A family-wide export_build job has `child_id` NULL (apps/api/src/routes/privacy.ts:808-812 inserts `child_id = ${childId}::uuid`, null for kind 'family_data'), so for a CHILD-scope deletion `child_id = p_child` evaluates to NULL and the job is NOT cancelled; a job already leased ('running') is not cancelled on either scope. (2) The builder's only deletion gate for a family-wide export is `childrenBeingDeleted()` (apps/api/src/jobs/export-build.ts:556-563, called at :445 for family_data and :345 for progress), which is an ordinary SELECT inside the build transaction under READ COMMITTED. If the deletion commits after that statement, the excluded-children array is empty and the deleted child's `child_profiles`, `assignments`, `extracted_questions` (prompt_text, student_answer_text, corrected_*), `question_results`, `attempts`, `points_ledger`, `child_feedback` and `safety_reports` rows all go into the file. (3) The settle is `update public.data_exports set status = 'ready', storage_path = ..., expires_at = now + 7 days where id = ... and status = 'queued'` (apps/api/src/jobs/export-build.ts:730-732). Its only guard is `status = 'queued'` — which the deletion left untouched — and it reads nothing about deletion. So the row flips to 'ready' with a live path and a 7-day expiry AFTER the deletion request. (4) apps/api/src/routes/export-download.ts:43-47 refuses only a non-'ready' row, a missing path or a lapsed expiry; the family is live and the caller's membership is active on a child-scope deletion, so `currentFamilyId` (apps/api/src/middleware/auth.ts:102-119) resolves and `assertRecentUnlock` is satisfied by the very unlock `request_deletion` itself required (0930:96-98). GET /v1/exports/:id/download therefore mints a signed URL for a file that holds the deleted child's homework. The window closes only when the deletion_purge job deletes the row (apps/api/src/jobs/dispatcher.ts:259-326 -> app.purge_family_data, supabase/migrations/0820_support_cases_purge.sql:121), i.e. one job tick — or, if that job dead-letters, until the 7-day sweep (dispatcher.ts:894-916). That is word for word the residual 0920's own header (0920:16-20) says it was written to remove. Secondary: 0920:29-30 cites `privacy.ts` for the builder's check; the check is in apps/api/src/jobs/export-build.ts, and for a FAMILY-scope deletion `childrenBeingDeleted` returns nothing at all (it requires `target_child_id is not null`, export-build.ts:558-562, and a family-scope request has target_child_id NULL), so for that scope the sentence "the builder leaves out every child with an open deletion request" is not merely racy, it is never true — the only family-scope guard is the handler's `join public.families f on f.deleted_at is null` at export-build.ts:691-693, taken once before the build starts.
findings.impact: A parent asks PencilLift to delete one child's data. An export that is being built at that moment completes, becomes downloadable with a 7-day link, and contains that child's homework prompts, the transcriptions of their answers, their grading verdicts and the fact that a safety notice was placed on a question — the data the deletion was supposed to stop. The product's own prose tells the parent the opposite: apps/api/src/routes/privacy.ts:336-344 states the withdrawal covers "every finished export file that holds the deleted data as soon as it is requested", and 0930:143-149 repeats it as the half that "must hold on every surface". Not rated high only because the recipient is the authenticated parent with a recent PIN unlock rather than a third party, and the purge normally closes it within one tick.
findings.ruled_out: (a) I checked whether the purge makes this moot: it does for the FILE (dispatcher.ts:283-294 removes the deterministic `exports/{family}/{id}.{ext}` paths of every non-'ready' row and re-schedules the pending ones in private.storage_removals at :310-325), but it closes the ROW only when it runs, which is the same tick-bounded/dead-letter-unbounded window HUNT6-B-2 was filed for. (b) I checked the handler's `withdrawExports` (privacy.ts:385-424): it runs once, after the RPC transaction, with the same `status = 'ready'` point-in-time predicate, so the API surface has the identical hole. (c) I checked whether the job cancel closes it: it does not, for the two reasons above (NULL child_id on a family-wide job; a leased job is 'running', not 'queued'). (d) I checked whether `app.guard_job()` (0600_operations.sql:109-124) stops the completion: its refusal fires only for `new.status in ('queued','running')`, so the dispatcher's own `set status = 'succeeded'` and the data_exports settle both pass. (e) I checked whether review/answer-key exports are affected: they always carry a non-null child_id, so export-build.ts:574-579 raises CHILD_DELETION_PENDING for them — only family-wide (child_id NULL) family_data/progress exports reach the hole. (f) I checked the FAMILY-scope variant for a download: `currentFamilyId` needs an active membership and 0930:129-130 revokes every one, so family scope leaks no download — the finding is child-scope. (g) I checked for a second download surface: `createSignedReadUrl` is reached from export-download.ts and scan-process.ts only; no admin route serves an export. (h) data_exports carries no append-only trigger and no FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, so the function's UPDATE is not being silently filtered — the statement really does what it says for 'ready' rows.
findings.reproduction: supabase/tests/hardening_r5_db.test.ts, case "expires the child's and the family-wide exports for a client-role call": its last assertion `expect(await exportRow(queued!.id)).toMatchObject({ status: 'queued' })` pins today's behaviour and is the line that has to be inverted. Add, immediately after the `request_deletion` call, the builder's own settle statement against that queued row — `update public.data_exports set status='ready', storage_path='exports/synthetic.json', expires_at=now()+interval '7 days' where id = ${queued.id} and status='queued' returning id` — and assert it returns no row. Today it returns the row and `exportRow(queued.id)` reads ('ready', <path>, lapsed=false), which is exactly what export-download.ts:43-47 admits.
findings.suggested_fix: Two halves, because the builder is the writer and the function is the backstop the Data API needs (L-037). (1) In a new migration (number is the lead's) regenerate `public.request_deletion` so the in-scope 'queued' rows are settled in the same transaction as the request — e.g. a second statement `update public.data_exports set status = 'failed' where family_id = p_family and status = 'queued' and (p_child is null or child_id = p_child or child_id is null)` — so the builder's `where ... and status = 'queued'` compare-and-set at export-build.ts:732 matches nothing and the file can never become downloadable. Correct 0920:29-30 and 0930:153-154 to name the real location of the builder's check (apps/api/src/jobs/export-build.ts) and to say that it covers child scope only and is evaluated before the build, not at settle time. (2) Because dispatcher.ts:283-294 builds its late-removal list from `status === 'queued'` alone, widen that filter to `status !== 'ready'` in the same change, or the newly 'failed' row loses its private.storage_removals entry and a file uploaded after the purge would be left behind. Belt and braces: make export-build.ts:730-732 a compare-and-set that also requires no open deletion request covering the export's children, so the builder refuses to publish a file the deletion has already invalidated.

findings.title: 0930 declares the canonical order and then claims the other writers "now agree with this function statement for statement"; they do not — child_sessions/child_devices and data_exports are both inverted against it
findings.claim_under_review: "The archive route, the billing writers and the purges (each: families `for update`, then the assignment, then the profile) now agree with this function statement for statement, and this function's own first lock is the family row ... So no cycle exists among the writers of this pair, by either route." (0930:76-80)
findings.mechanism: The second clause (no cycle among the writers of the PAIR) is true and I could not break it. The first clause is false, in two places. (a) The archive route writes, in this order, public.child_slot_assignments (apps/api/src/routes/family.ts:532), public.child_profiles (:535), public.child_sessions (:537), public.child_devices (:539). `public.request_deletion` writes public.child_sessions (0930:114), public.child_devices (0930:116), then the assignment (0930:137) and the profile (0930:140). So for {child_profiles, child_sessions} and for {child_slot_assignments, child_sessions} the two writers are inverted, not in agreement. (b) The purge, whose order 0930:10-11 cites as one of the three that agree, deletes public.child_slot_assignments (supabase/migrations/0820_support_cases_purge.sql:120), then public.data_exports (:121), then public.child_profiles (:123); this function updates the assignment, then the profile, then public.data_exports (0930:163) — an inversion of {child_profiles, data_exports} that 0920 introduced one migration earlier and that 0930's own sweep did not look at. What actually prevents a cycle in every one of these cases is the single fact stated in the second clause: the archive route, the billing writers and the purges all hold the family row FOR UPDATE (family.ts:66-76 lockFamily default mode; webhooks.ts:98-102 lockLiveFamily; billing.ts:319-322; billing-sync.ts:1461-1464; 0820:21), which conflicts with the FOR KEY SHARE that this function's first statement needs for `public.deletion_requests`' FK to `public.families` (0600_operations.sql:12). Statement agreement is not doing any of the work. The claim matters because 0930 exists precisely to replace 0890's too-narrow premise, and it names a live shape — `lockFamily(.., 'no-key-update')` at family.ts:439 — that does NOT conflict with FOR KEY SHARE. A writer of that shape that took child_profiles before child_sessions would deadlock against this function today (it locks C, the deletion locks session row S, the writer blocks on S, the deletion then blocks on C: 40P01), which the sentence says cannot happen. The next person who removes a lockFamily call, or adds a `for no key update` writer, will reason from a false premise — the exact failure 0890 -> 0930 is the record of.
findings.impact: No wrong outcome for a user today: every production writer of these rows serialises on the family row, so no deadlock and no 503 is reachable. The cost is to the next change. 0930 is the file that now defines "the canonical order" for this codebase, and it tells its reader that the deletion function and the archive route agree statement for statement, so the reader will not re-derive the family-row argument that is in fact the only protection — and will not notice that child_sessions, child_devices and data_exports are ordered the other way round.
findings.ruled_out: (a) I enumerated every writer of child_profiles and child_slot_assignments to be sure the second clause is sound and I am only disputing the first: activate (family.ts:467 lockFamily, :491 assignment insert, :492 profile), archive (:511 lockFamily), PATCH profile (:348 lockFamily), create child (:304 lockFamily), the pairing-code route (:439 lockFamily 'no-key-update', :442 child_profiles FOR NO KEY UPDATE, never the assignment), billing-sync applyCapacity then releaseSlotlessProfiles under all three FOR UPDATE callers, app.purge_family_data (0620/0710/0820, families FOR UPDATE first), app.inactivity_delete_family (0840:159 families FOR UPDATE, writes neither child row), and app.enforce_slot_capacity (0200_billing.sql:137-138), whose family FOR UPDATE is only ever reached on an insert made with the family row already locked. None contradicts the second clause. (b) I checked the Postgres row-lock matrix for the pairing-code route: FOR NO KEY UPDATE (held) vs FOR KEY SHARE (requested by the FK) is compatible, so the deletion really does pass the family row there — which is why the synthetic third case in hardening_r5_db.test.ts is a valid demonstration and why the sentence's scope matters. (c) I verified the round-6 diff really did only swap the two statements (diffed the 0920 and 0930 function bodies: the only change is the swap), so the inversions I name are not introduced by this migration — the false sentence about them is.
findings.reproduction: No test can go red for a false sentence; the check is the enumeration: apps/api/src/routes/family.ts:532-539 and supabase/migrations/0820_support_cases_purge.sql:120-123 against supabase/migrations/0930_deletion_lock_order.sql:114-168. If the fixer wants the claim guarded rather than corrected, the shape is hardening_r5_db.test.ts's third case with connection 1 taking `for no key update` on families, then `update public.child_profiles`, then `update public.child_sessions`: that deadlocks today (40P01), which 0930:76-80 says is impossible.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace 0930:76-80 with what is true and load-bearing: every other writer of these rows holds `public.families` FOR UPDATE before touching any child row, which conflicts with the FOR KEY SHARE this function's `insert into public.deletion_requests` takes for its foreign key, so no writer can interleave with it at all — and state that the assignment-before-profile order is a defensive convention for the pair only, not a statement-for-statement agreement, naming child_sessions, child_devices and data_exports as the rows where the two writers still differ and the family lock is the only protection. Keep the swapped statements (the code is right).

findings.title: The pl_child write invariant's column arm has an unplanted privilege: the column-level INSERT the case's own lead example names is the one grant no plant can see, so that word can be dropped and all five plants stay green
findings.claim_under_review: "`grant insert (id) on public.t to pl_child` is not in role_table_grants at all ... yet pl_child can insert rows naming just the granted columns. The migrations write parent grants in exactly that column-listing style, so the child-facing slip is one word away." (schema_invariants.test.ts:81-85), with "One plant per cell of the 2x2 matrix the query covers ... so no grantee can be dropped from either arm and stay green" (:106-112)
findings.mechanism: The query has four independent arms: two grantee lists (:95 table level, :100 column level) and two privilege lists (:96 table level, :101 column level). Round 6 added plant 5 (:171) and correctly pinned all four GRANTEE cells — I mutated each in turn and each goes red. The privilege list at :101 is `in ('INSERT','UPDATE')`, and both column-level plants are UPDATE: plant 3 at :139 (`grant update (metadata) ... to pl_child`) and plant 4 at :150 (`grant update (metadata) ... to public`). No plant is a column-level INSERT. Drop `'INSERT'` from :101 and every one of the five plants still returns exactly its expected single row — plant 1 (`grant insert on public.audit_events to public`, table level) survives because the table-level arm at :95-96 still names PUBLIC and INSERT — so the case stays green while `grant insert (metadata) on public.audit_events to pl_child` becomes invisible to `childWriteGrants()`. Nothing else in the file catches it: information_schema.role_table_grants carries table-level grants only, `has_table_privilege('pl_child', t, 'INSERT')` is false for a column-level grant, and the sibling '[DB-R2-04]' case (:182-215) covers only TRUNCATE, TRIGGER and REFERENCES. So the one grant shape the comment at :81-85 says the column arm exists for is the one the plants do not pin.
findings.impact: No live hole: the invariant as it stands does catch a column-level INSERT to pl_child or PUBLIC today. The cost is that the arm protecting family tables from a paired child's direct INSERT — the arm whose motivating example the comment writes out in full, and which CLAUDE.md's "child writes go through API-owned SECURITY DEFINER functions" rule depends on — is the one arm a future narrowing edit can delete with CI green, after which `grant insert (family_id, child_id) on public.<family table> to pl_child` would go unseen. That is the HUNT6-E-4 defect with one word moved.
findings.ruled_out: (a) I confirmed that information_schema.role_column_grants really does expand a TABLE-level INSERT/UPDATE/SELECT/REFERENCES grant to every column (information_schema.column_privileges unions the relacl-derived branch across pg_attribute), which is what makes plant 1 survive the mutation and is the same mechanism HUNT6-E-4 relied on for plant 3. (b) I checked each of the four grantee mutations to be sure the round-6 claim as written is TRUE and I am not re-filing E-4: dropping 'PUBLIC' from :95 reddens plant 2, 'pl_child' from :95 reddens plant 5, 'PUBLIC' from :100 reddens plant 4, 'pl_child' from :100 reddens plant 3. (c) I checked that TRUNCATE at :96 is covered elsewhere even though it too has no plant here — the '[DB-R2-04]' case names TRUNCATE for pl_child and PUBLIC — so INSERT at :101 is the only unpinned arm with no sibling coverage. (d) I checked the file is otherwise green and the plants are revoked in `finally`, so the mutation is genuinely silent rather than masked.
findings.reproduction: Mutate supabase/tests/schema_invariants.test.ts:101 to `and privilege_type in ('UPDATE')` and run `npx vitest run tests/schema_invariants.test.ts`: the case 'pl_child has no write privilege on any public table unless explicitly allowlisted' stays green on all five plants. In that state `grant insert (metadata) on public.audit_events to pl_child` yields zero rows from `childWriteGrants()`. Adding a sixth plant — `grant insert (metadata) on public.audit_events to pl_child` expecting `[{ table_name: 'audit_events', grantee: 'pl_child', privilege_type: 'INSERT' }]` — turns the mutation red.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the missing plant beside the other five, revoked in `finally` and followed by the empty re-assertion: `grant insert (metadata) on public.audit_events to pl_child` expecting the single `{ audit_events, pl_child, INSERT }` row. That is the only cell that pins `'INSERT'` into the column arm's privilege list, because a table-level INSERT reaches the table arm as well. While in the file, the same two-line addition closes the sibling gap the round-6 hunter recorded and did not file: the '[DB-R2-04]' case at :182-215 plants only a column-level REFERENCES to `authenticated`, so `'TRUNCATE'`, `'TRIGGER'` and the grantees anon/pl_child/PUBLIC in its table arm (:190-192) have no plant either. Do not narrow any arm.

findings.title: The reason 0920/0930 give for running the export withdrawal on FAMILY scope is false — no adult of a tombstoned family can reach the download route at all — and the other family-scope deletion writer, app.inactivity_delete_family, has no withdrawal
findings.claim_under_review: "The export withdrawal is NOT like that and runs for both scopes: a tombstoned family's adults keep a readable deletion state (0840) and the download route reads only data_exports, so a family-scope request must expire those rows as well." (0930:67-69, identical at 0920:41-44)
findings.mechanism: The sentence asserts that for a tombstoned family the download route would still serve a 'ready' export. It cannot. apps/api/src/routes/export-download.ts:31 calls `currentFamilyId(c)` BEFORE it reads public.data_exports at :35-38, and `currentFamilyId` (apps/api/src/middleware/auth.ts:102-118) resolves the caller's family from `public.family_memberships where user_id = ... and status = 'active'` and throws NOT_FOUND when there is none. A family-scope `request_deletion` revokes every active membership of that family in the same transaction (0930:129-130), and so does app.inactivity_delete_family (supabase/migrations/0840_hardening_r1_db.sql:189-191). So after either, every adult of that family gets 404 from GET /v1/exports/:id/download before data_exports is touched; if they belong to another family, `currentFamilyId` returns that family and the `and family_id = ${familyId}` clause at :37 still yields no row. The "readable deletion state (0840)" the sentence leans on is GET /v1/deletion (privacy.ts:712-735), which reads public.deletion_requests with the service role and never serves a file. The second half of the same reasoning was not carried through: `app.inactivity_delete_family` (0840:147-198) is the OTHER writer that files a family-scope deletion_requests row, and its body — deletion_requests, child_sessions, child_devices, jobs, assignments, families, family_memberships, the purge job, the audit row — contains no public.data_exports statement at all (grep of 0840 finds no `data_exports`), and privacy.ts's `withdrawExports` is not on that path either. If the stated reason were true, that path would be a live hole of the same class 0920 was written for; it is not a hole only because of `currentFamilyId`, a fact recorded nowhere.
findings.impact: No wrong outcome for a user: the family-scope arm of the withdrawal is harmless defence in depth, and the inactivity path's omission is covered because the purge deletes the rows (0820:121) and removes the files (dispatcher.ts:283-325). The cost is that the record now carries a false threat model for the deletion/export boundary. A reader given "the download route reads only data_exports" will conclude either that the inactivity path is broken (it is not) or that a future route may read data_exports without first resolving an active membership (which is the actual invariant, and it is written down nowhere) — and 0920's L-037 sweep stopped at `public.request_deletion` without saying that the second family-scope writer was considered.
findings.ruled_out: (a) I read the whole of export-download.ts to be sure `currentFamilyId` really is unavoidable and that no admin or child variant bypasses it; it is the only file that reads data_exports.storage_path for a caller, and `createSignedReadUrl` is otherwise reached only from scan-process.ts. (b) I checked that the membership revoke really covers every adult, not just the requester: the predicate is `where family_id = p_family and status = 'active'` (0930:129-130 and 0840:189-191). (c) I checked that the inactivity path's omission is not a live leak: the deletion_purge job it enqueues (0840:192-194) removes the export objects and app.purge_family_data deletes the rows, and `purgeExpiredExports` (dispatcher.ts:894-916) bounds anything it misses at the 7-day TTL. (d) I checked that this is not the same defect as HUNT7-D-1: that one is child-scope and reaches a real download; this one is family-scope prose plus an unswept surface, with no download reachable.
findings.reproduction: For the false reason there is no red test — it is a sentence about a route that cannot be reached, and the honest check is reading export-download.ts:31-38 with auth.ts:102-118. For the unswept surface, supabase/tests/jobs_hardening.test.ts already drives `app.inactivity_delete_family` (:224, :271, :350): seed a 'ready' data_exports row with a storage_path for that family before the call and assert `select status from public.data_exports` is 'expired' afterwards — that goes red today, and green for the same seed driven through `public.request_deletion(family, null)`.
findings.suggested_fix: Correct 0920:41-44 and 0930:67-69 to state the real reason the family-scope arm is kept — symmetry with the handler's `withdrawExports` and defence in depth against a future reader of data_exports that does not resolve an active membership first — and record the invariant that actually protects a tombstoned family today: apps/api/src/routes/export-download.ts resolves `currentFamilyId` before it reads the row, and a family-scope deletion revokes every active membership in the same transaction. Then either add the same withdrawal statement to `app.inactivity_delete_family` in the new migration HUNT7-D-1 already needs (it is the other writer of a family-scope deletion_requests row, and L-037 asks for the effect on every surface), or write down in 0840 and the ledger why it is deliberately left to the purge there. Do not remove the family-scope arm.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: 0940 cancels the GLOBAL PUBLIC default-privilege entry on sequences, which 0910's per-schema revoke cannot, and its test can tell the difference.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Traced the Postgres semantics (pg_default_acl keyed by defaclrole/defaclnamespace/defaclobjtype; get_user_default_acl merges the global row with the per-schema one, so a per-schema REVOKE can only subtract from the per-schema row) and then mutated every assertion of the new case at hardening_r2_db.test.ts:1294-1400 in my head: delete 0940's statement, drop the `after0910` arm, drop the premise, drop the effective-privilege arm. Also checked that `alter default privileges revoke all on sequences from public` writes no row when none exists (the computed ACL equals acldefault('S', owner), so the row is deleted/not created), and that defaclrole semantics mean the row that matters is the one belonging to the role that CREATES the sequence — i.e. the migration role — so 0940 is not defeated by the grantor problem that limits 0910:34.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Deleting 0940's single statement reddens both `expect(observed!.after0940Defaults).toEqual([])` and the three `usage:false, update:false` rows; the `after0910` arm is asserted rather than assumed, so the hole is demonstrated before the fix is applied; the premise `globalSequenceDefaults(tx)` is checked empty first, so nothing passes by inheritance; and the plant, the two probe sequences and the applied migration text all live inside a rolled-back transaction that the case then verifies is gone (relname like 'hr6_e2_%' count 0).

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The two widened default-privileges invariants see BOTH places a default can live, and each arm is pinned by a plant.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Dropped each arm of the rewritten queries at schema_invariants.test.ts:236-239 (tables) and :327-331 (sequences) in turn — the `n.nspname = 'public'` arm, the `d.defaclnamespace = 0` arm, and the left join itself — and checked which plant notices. Also checked the ACL-letter filter for tables (`acl.split('=')[1].split('/')[0]`) against the bare-grantee form `=Dxt/owner`, the named form `anon=arwdDxt/owner`, grant-option stars, and a grantor name that happens to contain D/x/t.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: The per-schema plant (:254-262) goes red if the nspname arm or the left join's `or` is dropped; the global plant (:265-277, and :347-357 for sequences) goes red if `defaclnamespace = 0` is dropped, and an inner join discards that row entirely. The letter filter reads the grantor half off before matching, so no grantor name can smuggle a letter in. I also confirmed the widening cannot false-positive in CI: the only `alter default privileges` statements in the tree are 0001:539 (global, objtype 'f' — filtered out by defaclobjtype), 0001:540/544 and 0860:99 and 0870:49 and 0910:60 (all `in schema`), and shim lines 107-109 (`in schema public`), so no global 'r' or 'S' row exists and the baselines stay empty.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The pl_child write invariant's completeness claim as REWRITTEN in round 6 — "no grantee can be dropped from either arm and stay green" over {PUBLIC, pl_child} x {table, column}.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Mutated each of the four grantee entries (schema_invariants.test.ts:95 and :100) and worked out which of the five plants notices, using the fact that information_schema.role_column_grants expands a table-level INSERT/UPDATE to every column (so a table-level plant can be caught by the column arm alone).
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Every grantee mutation reddens at least one plant: 'PUBLIC' out of the table arm reddens plant 2 (DELETE, no column form); 'pl_child' out of the table arm reddens plant 5 (the plant round 6 added); 'PUBLIC' out of the column arm reddens plant 4; 'pl_child' out of the column arm reddens plant 3. The round-6 fix for HUNT6-E-4 is correct and its rewritten comment is honest about being a claim over grantees. (The privilege lists are a separate matter — HUNT7-D-3.)

properties_attacked_and_held.property: No deadlock cycle exists among the writers of {public.child_slot_assignments, public.child_profiles} after 0930's swap.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Enumerated every writer of either row in the tree and wrote down the order and lock mode each takes: family.ts activate (:467 lockFamily FOR UPDATE, :491 assignment insert, :492 profile), archive (:511, :532, :535), PATCH profile (:348, :369), create child (:304, :316), the pairing-code route (:439 lockFamily 'no-key-update', :442 child_profiles FOR NO KEY UPDATE, no assignment), billing-sync applyCapacity (:689) then releaseSlotlessProfiles (:1316) under all three FOR UPDATE callers (webhooks.ts:98-102, billing.ts:319-322, billing-sync.ts:1461-1464), app.purge_family_data in 0620/0710/0820 (families FOR UPDATE first, then assignment, then profile), app.inactivity_delete_family (0840:159, neither child row), app.enforce_slot_capacity (0200:137-138), and request_deletion itself. Then checked the Postgres row-lock conflict matrix for each mode against the FOR KEY SHARE that `insert into public.deletion_requests` takes on public.families (and on public.child_profiles, via the composite FK at 0600_operations.sql:23), and checked that the partial unique index child_slot_assignments_one_open makes a concurrent open-slot insert WAIT rather than fail.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Every writer that touches both rows holds the family row FOR UPDATE before either, which conflicts with the deletion's FOR KEY SHARE, so the two can never interleave past the deletion's first statement. The one live FOR NO KEY UPDATE holder (the pairing-code route) locks child_profiles and never writes child_slot_assignments, and FOR NO KEY UPDATE is compatible with the FOR KEY SHARE the FK takes, so no cycle closes either way. The third case in hardening_r5_db.test.ts is a genuine mutation-sensitive demonstration: with 0890's order reverted it deadlocks (the deletion would hold child_profiles while blocking on the assignment) and both `expect(codes).toEqual(['ok','ok'])` and `not.toContain('child_profiles')` go red.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The 0910 idempotency case now pins both of 0910's statements and both of 0870's (the HUNT6-E-5 repair).
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Checked whether each new arm can be dropped: the (b) block's `twice.first.acl.filter(/[{,]=/)` over every sequence's relacl, the `twice.first.defaults.filter(startsWith('='))`, the (a) before/after snapshot, and the two `toContain` assertions on 0870's text. Also checked whether re-applying 0910 on the deployed schema can itself change state (a REVOKE materialises a NULL relacl) and whether the plant can escape the transaction.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Deleting 0910:59 reddens the relacl arm; deleting 0910:60 reddens the defaults arm; deleting either 0870 statement now reddens (c). The deployed sequences already carry explicit ACLs from 0870:44 and 0910:34, so the (a) snapshot is stable across a re-application, and the (b) block is inside a rolled-back transaction. The non-grantor case is honest about what it pins (a Postgres semantic, typed literally rather than read from the migration) and its role/schema fixture is verified gone afterwards.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The migration sequence tolerates the gap left by deleting 0880.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Read supabase/scripts/migrate.ts (listMigrations is `readdir` + `.filter(endsWith('.sql'))` + `.sort()`), harness.ts's PL_MIGRATIONS_ONLY prefix filter, and grepped the whole tree for anything that counts, checksums, hashes or assumes contiguity of migration file names, plus every remaining reference to 0880 or its column and index.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Nothing enumerates migrations except by lexicographic readdir; there is no ledger table, count assertion or checksum, and the prefix filter matches by string prefix, so a gap is invisible. The only surviving reference to 0880 is the deliberate absence test at hardening_r1_db2.test.ts:523-556, which reads the real table (its `arrayContaining(['id','session_id','token_hash','used_at','replaced_by'])` anchor makes both negatives non-vacuous). No `used_request_id` remains in any migration, route, job or script.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The raised floors in scripts/test-minimums.json are all below the count a full run produces, and none can be met by a suite that did not run.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Reconstructed the db count independently: 381 static `it(`/`test(` declarations across supabase/tests, plus the expansion of amazon_channel.test.ts's `describe.each(CHANNEL_COLUMNS)` x (`it.each([...OLD_CHANNELS, NEW_CHANNEL])` + 1) — 2 static lines becoming N x 5 real tests — which reconciles exactly with the 429 recorded in docs/Test_Evidence.md:63. Checked every floor against its recorded count (407/429, 1098/1156, 793/835, 746/786, 76/80, 19/20, 3473/3656, 4/4) and read scripts/assert-test-count.mjs for how a filtered or partial run is treated.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: Every floor is at or just under 95% of the measured count, so none is above what a legitimate full run produces; the audit also fails on any failed, pending or todo test and on a missing report, so a suite that silently did not run cannot satisfy it, and `PL_MIGRATIONS_ONLY` runs are not gated because the audit only runs after the full `pnpm check`. The supabase package really is `@pencillift/db` with a `test` script, so it is one of the packages the audit walks.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: The new data_exports UPDATE inside the SECURITY DEFINER function is not silently filtered or blocked.

The `now()` choice matches every other timestamp in the same function; 0780 converted only `public.jobs.run_after`, and the operative half of the withdrawal is the status, which no clock affects.

properties_attacked_and_held.property: 0940's claim that it need add nothing for sequences that already exist, and that on a database without a global default it writes no row.
properties_attacked_and_held.how_you_attacked_it: Looked for the gap the reasoning leaves: a sequence created by a migration numbered between 0910 (which revokes on existing sequences) and 0940 (which only fixes the default) would, on a database carrying a global PUBLIC default, keep the privilege with nothing to clean it and only a CI-invisible invariant to report it.
properties_attacked_and_held.why_it_held: The gap is empty and stays empty: 0920 and 0930 only `create or replace function` and create no relation, and migration numbering is monotonic, so any future migration that adds an identity column is numbered above 0940 and runs after the global revoke. I did not file it.

findings.title: ACCOUNT_CLOSE_COPY.pending blames a family purge for every `pending` closure, but a guardian gets `pending` when the auth service refuses — and the round-6 SIGN_OUT_NOT_TOLD_COPY doc rests on that same premise
findings.claim_under_review: `pending: 'Your request is recorded. Your sign-in closes automatically once your family account’s deletion has finished, and this device is signed out now.'` and the round-6 JSDoc on SIGN_OUT_NOT_TOLD_COPY.signInOpen: "(ordinary sign-out; and the `pending` closure, where the sign-in stays usable until the family purge finishes)"
findings.mechanism: apps/api/src/routes/account.ts:104-110: when `owned` is null (an invited guardian, or an adult with no family) the route calls `closeNow`, and `closeNow` (account.ts:181-200) returns false on any throw from `authAdmin.closeUser`, so the route answers `{ status: 'pending', signOut: true }` with 202. That branch is the documented, tested guardian-refusal path (apps/api/tests/account-close.test.ts:246-262 'guardian path when the auth service refuses'), and account.ts's own header states it: "`pending` only when the closing service was unreachable, in which case the queued job retries". Every surface then renders the family-purge sentence for it: apps/web/src/pages/app/PrivacyControlsPage.tsx:766 sets the outcome to `ACCOUNT_CLOSE_COPY.pending`; apps/web/src/pages/public/AccountDeletionPage.tsx:78 renders it after the navigate at PrivacyControlsPage.tsx:837; `stillSignedInCopy` (PrivacyControlsPage.tsx:723-728) inlines the same clause; apps/mobile/src/privacy/parent-privacy.ts:190-206 returns `ACCOUNT_CLOSE_COPY.pending` or its own variant carrying the same clause. For that guardian there is no family deletion at all — `removeGuardian` (account.ts:117-141) only revokes their own membership and the family stays live — so the sentence names an event that will never happen, and the real mechanism (the `account_close` job retrying, account-close.test.ts:263-270) is never mentioned.
findings.impact: A guardian (or an adult with no family) who deletes their account during an auth-provider outage is told their sign-in closes 'once your family account’s deletion has finished'. They have no family account deletion and can see none, so the only reasonable reading is that nothing will close their sign-in. They then find they can still sign in, with no honest account of why or of when it ends. The round-6 change made this premise load-bearing: `serverNotTold` (AccountDeletionPage.tsx:57-61) now branches on exactly this flag, and its contract JSDoc states the premise as fact.
findings.ruled_out: I checked that the password half of the round-6 copy is still correct on this path — the sign-in genuinely does still exist, so `signInOpen`'s 'change your password if you are worried' is a real remedy (apps/web/src/pages/auth/UpdatePasswordPage.tsx and ResetPasswordPage.tsx exist), which is why this finding is about the attribution, not the remedy. I checked that a completed closure really does end sessions (apps/api/src/providers/auth-admin.ts:19-20, soft delete with sessions ended), so `signInClosed`'s 'nothing left to do' is true and only the `pending` string is wrong. I checked that the guardian is not left permanently open: enqueueClose (account.ts:147-175) queues an `account_close` job that retries, so the OUTCOME is right and only the explanation is false. I checked that the owner path (the one the copy describes) is a separate early return at account.ts:104-107, so the two cases really do share one string.
findings.reproduction: apps/web/src/pages/app/PrivacyControlsPage.test.tsx — render the close flow for a guardian whose POST /v1/account/close answers `{status:'pending'}` and assert the notice does not claim the sign-in closes once a family deletion finishes; the same case for apps/mobile/src/privacy/parent-privacy.test.ts against `accountClosedDeviceMessage('pending', …)`. Both go red today on the rendered text.
findings.suggested_fix: Have POST /v1/account/close say WHY it is pending (the response is a strict object, so add a discriminator such as `reason: 'after_family_purge' | 'retrying'`, set from whether `owned` was non-null versus `closeNow` having returned false), and split ACCOUNT_CLOSE_COPY.pending into the two sentences that follow from it — the owner's 'once your family account’s deletion has finished' and the retry case's 'we could not finish closing it just now; it closes automatically within a few minutes'. Correct the SIGN_OUT_NOT_TOLD_COPY.signInOpen JSDoc to say what `pending` actually means (the sign-in still exists, for either reason) rather than naming the family purge.
